units.title: Matter, Measurement & Lab Safety
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A sealed bag of microwave popcorn increases in size when heated but does not change in mass. What is happening to the matter inside?
essential_questions: How can we classify different types of matter based on their properties?
Why is precise measurement important in scientific investigation?
What safety protocols protect us during laboratory work?
units.crse_theme: Students explore how cultural practices around food preparation (e.g., nixtamalization of corn, fermentation in kimchi) involve chemical and physical changes, connecting indigenous and global knowledge systems to chemistry concepts.
investigations: Investigation 1: Classifying Unknown Substances by Physical Properties

lessons.title: Classifying Matter: Pure Substances vs. Mixtures
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify matter as a pure substance or mixture and further distinguish between elements, compounds, homogeneous mixtures, and heterogeneous mixtures based on observable properties.
lessons.circle_prompt: Share a time when something changed form but was still the same thing underneath.
lessons.do_now: Look at the four items on your desk (salt, sand, a penny, and trail mix). Sort them into two groups and be ready to explain your reasoning.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Sample set per group: salt, sand, iron filings, trail mix, distilled water

engage.description: Show a short video clip of a street food vendor making cotton candy. Ask: Is cotton candy the same substance as the sugar that went in? Students turn-and-talk, then share out. Chart initial ideas on the board.

explore.description: In groups of 3, students examine the sample set using hand lenses and magnets. They record observations in a T-chart (what they see vs. what they infer about composition). Groups attempt to sort substances into categories and post their sorting criteria on sticky notes.

explain.description: Teacher-led discussion building the classification hierarchy: Matter splits into Pure Substances (Elements, Compounds) and Mixtures (Homogeneous, Heterogeneous). Students label their samples using the new vocabulary and complete the graphic organizer with definitions and examples for each category.

elaborate.description: Students receive three new mystery samples (bronze coin, carbonated water, granite rock) and must classify them using the framework. They write a justification sentence for each using the Because/But/So structure.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a description of a substance (e.g., 'a clear liquid that boils at 100 degrees C and is composed of hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded'), students identify it as element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture and provide one piece of supporting evidence.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled graphic organizer with key terms and definitions already placed; pair with a peer mentor during the Explore phase for guided observation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the classification activity as designed with the graphic organizer scaffold.
differentiation.advanced: Challenge students to propose a method to separate each mixture and explain the physical principle behind each separation technique (filtration, distillation, chromatography).
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual vocabulary list (Spanish/English) with diagrams; use visual cues on the classification chart; allow verbal responses during the Evaluate phase.
differentiation.iep: Extended time on exit ticket; preferential seating near the anchor chart; provide a word bank for all written responses.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how indigenous peoples across the Americas classified natural materials (plants, minerals, animal products) for medicine, construction, and art long before modern chemistry formalized these categories. Highlight Mayan use of indigo dye extraction as an early separation technique.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'heterogeneous mixture': Trail mix is a heterogeneous mixture because___. Trail mix contains different visible components, but___. Trail mix is made of physically combined ingredients, so___.

vocabulary.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space
Matter with a fixed composition that cannot be separated by physical means
A pure substance made of only one type of atom
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
Two or more substances physically combined that retain their individual properties
A mixture with uniform composition throughout, also called a solution
A mixture with visibly different parts or phases

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is Matter?
Section 2: Pure Substances — Elements vs. Compounds
Section 3: Mixtures — Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous
Section 4: Classification Flowchart — How to Identify Unknown Samples

cer.phenomenon: You are given three unknown white powders labeled A, B, and C. Powder A dissolves completely in water and the solution conducts electricity. Powder B does not dissolve and feels gritty. Powder C dissolves in water but the solution does not conduct electricity.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the observed physical properties, I claim that Powder A is classified as a___, Powder B is classified as a___, and Powder C is classified as a___.
cer.evidence_source: Use data from the observations table (solubility, conductivity, texture) to identify at least two properties per substance that support your classification.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the physical properties of Powder [letter] are consistent with a [category], which is defined as___. For example, [property] indicates___ because___.

lessons.title: Physical vs. Chemical Properties and Changes
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between physical and chemical properties and identify evidence that a physical or chemical change has occurred.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is something you cooked, built, or created recently? Did you change the materials permanently or could you undo it?
lessons.do_now: Look at the two images projected on the board: ice melting in a glass, and a piece of paper burning. Write one similarity and one difference between these two events.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Lab stations: candle and matches, steel wool and vinegar, baking soda and vinegar, ice cubes, sugar
Physical vs. Chemical Changes data table (printed)

engage.description: Demonstration: Teacher tears a piece of paper in half, then burns another piece. Ask: Both pieces of paper changed. What is fundamentally different about these two changes? Students record predictions in notebooks.

explore.description: Station rotation (4 stations, 3 min each): Station 1 — melt ice and record temperature; Station 2 — place steel wool in vinegar and observe; Station 3 — mix baking soda and vinegar, observe gas production; Station 4 — dissolve sugar in warm water. Students record observations (color change, gas production, temperature change, precipitate) in the data table.

explain.description: Teacher guides students to categorize each station as physical or chemical change using the evidence they gathered. Build a class anchor chart listing indicators of chemical change (gas production, color change, temperature change, precipitate formation, light/sound). Define physical and chemical properties with examples from the stations.

elaborate.description: Students watch a 2-minute clip of bread baking and list at least three pieces of evidence that chemical changes are occurring. Then they identify two physical changes that also happen during baking (shape change, moisture evaporation).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Students read three scenarios (rusting nail, crushing a can, frying an egg) and classify each as physical or chemical change, citing specific evidence from the lesson's indicator list.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-labeled data table with observation prompts at each station (e.g., 'Look for: color change? yes/no; Gas bubbles? yes/no'); include a reference card listing the five indicators of chemical change.
differentiation.on_level: Complete station rotation and classification activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: For each station, students write the chemical equation if it is a chemical change, or explain at the molecular level why the physical change is reversible.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual anchor chart with photographs of each indicator of chemical change labeled in English and Spanish; use sentence frames for exit ticket responses.
differentiation.iep: Reduce stations to 3 instead of 4; allow partner work for data recording; provide a graphic organizer that sorts observations into physical vs. chemical columns.

lessons.crse_connection: Connection to food chemistry across cultures: tortilla-making (nixtamalization is a chemical change that makes niacin bioavailable), fermentation in kimchi, yogurt, and injera. Highlight how communities discovered chemical processes through observation centuries before formal chemistry.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'chemical change': Burning wood is a chemical change because___. Dissolving salt in water looks like a change, but___. A new substance with different properties formed, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A characteristic of matter that can be observed or measured without changing the substance's identity
A characteristic that describes a substance's ability to change into a different substance
A change in matter that alters its form or appearance but not its chemical composition
A change that produces one or more new substances with different properties from the original
A solid that forms when two solutions are mixed
Observable evidence such as color change, gas production, temperature change, or precipitate formation that suggests a new substance has formed

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Physical Properties and Examples
Section 2: Chemical Properties and Examples
Section 3: Physical Changes — Reversible Transformations
Section 4: Chemical Changes — Five Key Indicators
Section 5: Classifying Changes Using Evidence

cer.phenomenon: A student heats a spoonful of sugar slowly over a flame. At first the sugar melts into a clear liquid, then it turns brown, gives off a smell, and eventually becomes a black solid. The student claims that only a chemical change occurred.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that heating sugar involves both___ and___ changes because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use observations from the sugar-heating description and data from the station rotation lab to identify specific indicators of each type of change.
cer.reasoning_frame: The initial melting is a___ change because___. However, the browning and odor indicate a___ change because___, which means new substances with different properties were formed.

lessons.title: Measurement, SI Units, and Significant Figures
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can take accurate measurements using appropriate SI units and express them with the correct number of significant figures.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is one measurement you made today before coming to school — time, distance, amount of food? How precise was it?
lessons.do_now: Estimate the length of your desk in centimeters. Write your estimate, then measure with a ruler. How close were you? Why might your estimate differ from your measurement?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Graduated cylinders (10 mL and 100 mL per group)
Irregular objects for volume measurement (small rocks, metal bolts)

engage.description: Tell the story of the NASA Mars Climate Orbiter — a $125 million spacecraft lost because one team used metric units and another used English units. Show a diagram of the failed trajectory. Ask: Why do scientists around the world agree on one measurement system?

explore.description: Station rotation (4 stations, ~3.5 min each): Station 1 — measure the length of three objects with a ruler to the correct decimal place; Station 2 — mass three objects on a triple-beam balance; Station 3 — measure liquid volumes using a 10 mL and 100 mL graduated cylinder (read the meniscus); Station 4 — find the volume of an irregular solid by water displacement. Students record all measurements with proper units.

explain.description: Introduce significant figures: rules for counting sig figs (nonzero digits, captive zeros, trailing zeros with decimals). Students revisit their measurements and determine the correct number of sig figs for each. Brief discussion: Why do different tools give different levels of precision?

elaborate.description: Practice problems: Students calculate density using their measurements from the Explore phase and express answers with the correct number of significant figures using the multiplication/division rule (answer has the fewest sig figs of any measurement used).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Three questions — (1) How many sig figs in 0.00340? (2) A student measures mass as 12.5 g and volume as 3.2 mL. Express the density with the correct sig figs. (3) Explain in one sentence why sig figs matter.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a measurement checklist at each station with step-by-step instructions (e.g., 'Step 1: Place object on balance. Step 2: Slide riders until balanced. Step 3: Read and record mass.'); include a sig fig rules card with color-coded examples.
differentiation.on_level: Complete station rotation and sig fig practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate percent error for each measurement compared to accepted values and analyze which measurement tools introduce the most uncertainty.
differentiation.ell: Label all measurement tools with diagrams showing how to read them in English and native language; provide sentence frames for the quick-write evaluation.
differentiation.iep: Allow use of calculator for all sig fig problems; provide extra time at stations; reduce practice problems from 6 to 3; enlarged sig fig reference card.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how ancient civilizations developed precise measurement systems — Egyptian cubits for pyramid construction, Chinese chi for silk trade, Aztec measurement based on body proportions. Discuss how measurement standards reflect cultural needs and values, and how the metric system was created during the French Revolution as a 'democratic' system of measurement.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: Students write sentences embedding a definition as an appositive. 'Significant figures, the meaningful digits in a measurement that include all certain digits plus one estimated digit, tell us how precise our tools are.' 'The meniscus, the curved surface of a liquid in a container, must be read at eye level for an accurate volume measurement.'

vocabulary.definition: The digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus one estimated digit
How close repeated measurements are to each other
How close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
The curved surface of a liquid in a graduated cylinder, read at the bottom of the curve
The International System of Units used by scientists worldwide (meter, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole)
The ratio of an object's mass to its volume, expressed as g/mL or g/cm cubed

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why Measurement Matters — The SI System
Section 2: Measuring Length, Mass, Volume, and Temperature
Section 3: Rules for Counting Significant Figures
Section 4: Significant Figures in Calculations (Addition vs. Multiplication Rules)

cer.phenomenon: Two lab groups measure the density of the same aluminum block. Group A reports 2.9 g/mL using a basic scale and a beaker for water displacement. Group B reports 2.71 g/mL using a digital balance and a graduated cylinder. The accepted density of aluminum is 2.70 g/mL.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Group___ obtained a more accurate result because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare each group's result to the accepted value, calculate percent error, and identify which measurement tools provided more significant figures.
cer.reasoning_frame: Group B's result is more accurate because their tools provided [number] significant figures compared to Group A's [number], so their measurement had greater precision. This demonstrates that___ because___.

lessons.title: Lab Safety, Equipment, and Scientific Investigation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify proper lab safety procedures, demonstrate correct use of common lab equipment, and design a basic investigation with appropriate controls.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever had a close call where following (or not following) safety rules made a difference? What did you learn?
lessons.do_now: Look at the projected image of a messy lab setup with 5 safety violations circled. Identify each violation and explain what the student should do instead.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Safety equipment: goggles, aprons, fire extinguisher, eyewash station, fire blanket
Common lab equipment set per group: beaker, Erlenmeyer flask, test tube, watch glass, ring stand, Bunsen burner (unlit)

engage.description: Show a short compilation of lab accident clips (appropriate for high school) from safety training videos. Ask: What went wrong in each case? Could it have been prevented? Students identify the safety rule violated in each clip.

explore.description: Equipment scavenger hunt: In groups of 3, students rotate through 6 stations, each featuring 2-3 pieces of lab equipment. At each station, students sketch the equipment, write its name, and describe its purpose. Groups also locate all safety equipment in the room (eyewash, fire extinguisher, fire blanket, exits) and mark them on a room map.

explain.description: Teacher reviews lab safety rules organized by category: (1) Personal protection (goggles, aprons, hair), (2) Chemical handling (never taste, waft to smell, read labels), (3) Heat/fire safety (Bunsen burner protocol, hot glass looks like cold glass), (4) Emergency procedures (eyewash, fire blanket, broken glass). Students complete a safety rules graphic organizer.

elaborate.description: Safety scenario challenge: Each group receives 3 scenario cards describing lab situations (e.g., 'A student spills acid on their hand' or 'The student at the next bench has long hair near a Bunsen burner'). Groups discuss and write the correct safety response for each, then present one scenario to the class.

evaluate.description: Lab safety quiz: 10 multiple-choice and short-answer questions covering safety symbols, emergency procedures, and equipment identification. Students who pass sign the lab safety contract.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a labeled equipment reference sheet with photographs during the scavenger hunt; use a matching format for the safety quiz instead of open-ended questions.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the safety scavenger hunt and quiz as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Students design a safety poster for one specific lab procedure (heating a test tube, diluting an acid) that could be displayed in the classroom, including a step-by-step protocol with warnings.
differentiation.ell: Provide safety rules with visual icons and bilingual labels; allow oral assessment of safety procedures as an alternative to the written quiz.
differentiation.iep: Chunked safety quiz with one category per section; allow use of safety reference sheet during the quiz; pair with a peer for the scavenger hunt.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the historical lack of safety protections for workers of color in chemical industries — the Hawks Nest Tunnel disaster (1930s, West Virginia) where hundreds of Black workers died from silica dust exposure without protective equipment. Connect to the importance of safety advocacy and environmental justice.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Goggles protect.' Students expand with when, where, why, and how: 'In the chemistry lab, safety goggles, which are made of impact-resistant polycarbonate, protect students' eyes from chemical splashes and flying debris whenever they handle liquids or heat substances.'

vocabulary.definition: A safety device that provides a gentle stream of water to rinse chemicals from the eyes for at least 15 minutes
Material Safety Data Sheet — a document that lists hazards, handling procedures, and first aid for each chemical
The safe technique of using your hand to gently fan vapors toward your nose to detect odor instead of directly inhaling
A factor in an experiment that is kept the same to ensure a fair test
A cone-shaped glass container with a narrow neck used for mixing and heating liquids

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
Section 2: Chemical Handling and Disposal Rules
Section 3: Heat and Fire Safety Procedures
Section 4: Emergency Protocols and Equipment Location
Section 5: Common Lab Equipment — Names and Uses

cer.phenomenon: A student wants to investigate which metal (iron, copper, or zinc) reacts most vigorously with hydrochloric acid. They plan to pour acid into three beakers, add a different metal to each, and observe. Their teacher says the procedure is incomplete.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's procedure is missing the following safety precautions and experimental controls:___.
cer.evidence_source: Reference the lab safety rules from class and identify at least two safety issues and two experimental design flaws in the student's plan.
cer.reasoning_frame: The student needs to add___ because without it,___. Additionally, the experiment requires___ as a control so that___, which ensures the results are valid.

lessons.title: Separation Techniques and Matter Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can select and justify an appropriate separation technique for a given mixture based on the physical properties of its components.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to separate a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings using only household items, what would you try first and why?
lessons.do_now: A gold miner in the 1800s needed to separate gold flakes from river sand. Describe one method they might have used and explain what physical property makes it work.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Mixture per group: sand, salt, iron filings, small pebbles
Separation tools: magnets, filter paper, funnels, beakers, ring stands, evaporating dishes, hot plates
Safety goggles and aprons (1 per student)

engage.description: Show images of real-world separation: a water treatment plant, panning for gold, oil-water separators after a spill. Ask: What physical property is being exploited in each case? Students pair-share their ideas.

explore.description: Challenge lab: Each group receives a mixture of sand, salt, iron filings, and pebbles. Their task is to separate the mixture into its four pure components using available tools. Groups must plan their separation sequence before beginning (write steps on a whiteboard) and recover as much of each component as possible.

explain.description: Class debrief: Groups share their separation sequence. Teacher formalizes the techniques — magnetism (for magnetic materials), filtration (for insoluble solids from liquids), evaporation (for dissolved solids from solution), distillation (for liquids with different boiling points), chromatography (for pigments/dyes). For each technique, identify the physical property that makes it work.

elaborate.description: Application problems: Students receive three real-world mixture scenarios (desalinating seawater, separating blood components in a hospital, extracting caffeine from coffee) and must identify the best separation technique and the physical property it depends on.

evaluate.description: Unit 1 review exit ticket: Five cumulative questions covering matter classification, physical vs. chemical changes, measurement/sig figs, and separation techniques.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a flowchart decision tree: 'Is any component magnetic? If yes, start with a magnet.' Guide students through the separation sequence step-by-step with prompts.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the separation challenge with the planning whiteboard and reference sheet as designed.
differentiation.advanced: After completing the separation, students calculate percent recovery for each component and write an error analysis explaining any mass lost.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual separation techniques chart with labeled diagrams and bilingual descriptions; use sentence starters for the elaborate section.
differentiation.iep: Pre-printed separation steps that students arrange in order rather than writing from scratch; reduce elaborate section to two scenarios instead of three.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how water purification has been practiced across cultures for thousands of years — ancient Egyptian sand filtration, Ayurvedic copper vessel water treatment, and modern-day challenges with clean water access in communities like Flint, Michigan. Connect separation science to environmental justice.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'filtration': Filtration can separate sand from salt water because___. Filtration works for insoluble solids, but___. The salt dissolved completely in water, so filtration alone cannot___.

vocabulary.definition: A separation technique that uses a porous barrier to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
A separation technique that removes a liquid from a dissolved solid by heating until the liquid changes to gas
A separation technique that uses differences in boiling points to separate a mixture of liquids
A separation technique that separates components of a mixture based on their different rates of movement through a medium
A physical property that allows certain metals like iron, nickel, and cobalt to be attracted to a magnet
The ability of a substance to dissolve in a solvent, measured as the maximum amount that dissolves at a given temperature

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why Separation Matters — Real-World Applications
Section 2: Separation by Physical Properties (Magnetism, Density, Solubility, Boiling Point)
Section 3: Techniques — Filtration, Evaporation, Distillation, Chromatography
Section 4: Choosing the Right Technique — Decision Flowchart

cer.phenomenon: A community's only water source is a lake that contains dissolved salt, suspended clay particles, and algae floating on the surface. The community needs to produce clean drinking water using available resources.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the community should use the following sequence of separation techniques to purify the water:___.
cer.evidence_source: For each contaminant, identify the physical property that differs from water and match it to the appropriate separation technique from your notes.
cer.reasoning_frame: First, ___ should be removed by___ because its physical property of___ allows it to be separated. Next,___ because___. Finally,___ so that the remaining dissolved salt is removed.

units.title: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Neon signs glow in different colors depending on the gas inside the tube. Why do different elements emit different colors of light when energized?
essential_questions: How has our model of the atom changed over time and what evidence drove those changes?
How does the arrangement of electrons in an atom determine its chemical behavior?
Why are elements organized the way they are on the periodic table, and what patterns emerge?
units.crse_theme: Students explore contributions of scientists from diverse backgrounds to atomic theory, including Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table, Chien-Shiung Wu's work on nuclear physics, and the use of spectroscopy in West African gold assaying traditions.

summative: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration Test

investigations: Investigation 2: Flame Test Lab — Identifying Elements by Their Emission Spectra
Investigation 3: Periodic Trends Graphing and Analysis

lessons.title: History of Atomic Models: Dalton to Thomson
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe Dalton's atomic theory and Thomson's plum pudding model, and explain what experimental evidence led to each model.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you changed your mind about something because you got new information. What convinced you?
lessons.do_now: Imagine you have a box you cannot open. How would you figure out what is inside without looking? List three strategies.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Black boxes with hidden objects (1 per group)

engage.description: Black box activity: Each group shakes, tilts, and rolls a sealed box containing a hidden object. They make inferences about what is inside based on indirect evidence. Debrief: This is exactly how scientists studied the atom — they could never see it directly but designed experiments to infer its structure.

explore.description: Jigsaw reading: Students split into expert groups. Group A reads about Democritus and the Greek concept of 'atomos.' Group B reads about Dalton's atomic theory (1808) and his five postulates. Group C reads about Thomson's cathode ray experiment and discovery of the electron. Each group creates a summary card with the scientist, date, key experiment, model drawing, and what the model explained.

explain.description: Students return to home groups and teach each other. Teacher guides whole-class construction of a timeline, emphasizing that each model was an improvement based on new experimental evidence. Key points: Dalton's solid sphere model; Thomson's discovery that atoms contain negative charges (electrons) embedded in positive material — the plum pudding model.

elaborate.description: Students draw and label both the Dalton model and the Thomson model. They write a comparison paragraph explaining what Thomson's model could explain that Dalton's could not (the existence of charged particles within the atom, electrical behavior of matter).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) List two postulates of Dalton's atomic theory. (2) What experimental evidence did Thomson use to revise Dalton's model? (3) Draw and label the plum pudding model.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed timeline with dates and scientist names already filled in; students add the model drawing and key evidence. Include guiding questions for the jigsaw reading.
differentiation.on_level: Complete jigsaw reading and timeline construction as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research which of Dalton's original postulates have since been modified or disproven (e.g., atoms are indivisible, all atoms of an element are identical) and explain what evidence led to the revision.
differentiation.ell: Provide jigsaw readings at a reduced Lexile level with key vocabulary bolded and defined in margins; allow model drawings with labeled diagrams instead of written paragraphs.
differentiation.iep: Pre-printed summary cards with fill-in-the-blank format instead of open-ended writing; seated near the projected timeline for reference; extended time on exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how ancient Indian philosopher Kanada (6th century BCE) proposed that matter is made of indivisible particles called 'paramanu' — predating Greek atomism. Highlight how multiple cultures independently developed atomic concepts, challenging the Eurocentric narrative of scientific discovery.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'atomic model': Dalton proposed that atoms are indivisible spheres because___. Thomson discovered electrons in the cathode ray experiment, but Dalton's model had no subatomic particles, so___. Scientists revised the atomic model because___.

vocabulary.definition: The smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element
The scientific theory that all matter is composed of atoms
A negatively charged subatomic particle found outside the nucleus
A stream of electrons observed traveling from the negative electrode to the positive electrode in a vacuum tube
Thomson's model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Ancient Ideas About Matter — Democritus and Kanada
Section 2: Dalton's Atomic Theory — Five Key Postulates
Section 3: Thomson's Cathode Ray Experiment
Section 4: The Plum Pudding Model — Atoms Have Internal Structure

cer.phenomenon: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, it becomes positively charged and can attract small pieces of paper. Dalton's model describes atoms as solid, indivisible spheres with no internal structure.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Dalton's atomic model cannot fully explain the phenomenon of static electricity because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use evidence from Thomson's cathode ray experiment and observations about charged objects to support your reasoning.
cer.reasoning_frame: Static electricity requires the transfer of___ between objects. Dalton's model cannot explain this because___. Thomson's model improved on this because___, which means___.

lessons.title: Rutherford, Bohr, and the Quantum Mechanical Model
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can compare the Rutherford, Bohr, and quantum mechanical models of the atom and explain what evidence supported each revision.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could discover a new element, what would you name it and why?
lessons.do_now: If Thomson's plum pudding model were correct, what would happen if you shot tiny positive particles at a thin sheet of gold foil? Draw your prediction.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Gold foil experiment simulation (PhET or projected animation)

engage.description: Show an animation of Rutherford's gold foil experiment. Before revealing results, ask students to predict: If the atom is a uniform blob of positive charge (Thomson), what path should alpha particles take? Students sketch predictions. Then reveal the actual results — most pass through, some deflect, a few bounce back. Students react: What does this tell us?

explore.description: Data analysis: Students receive a simplified data table showing the percentage of alpha particles that passed straight through (99%), deflected slightly (0.9%), and bounced back (0.01%). In pairs, they answer guided questions: What must the atom mostly be? (empty space) Where is the positive charge concentrated? (tiny, dense center) What did Rutherford call this center? (nucleus) Students draw the nuclear model.

explain.description: Teacher presents the progression: Rutherford's nuclear model (electrons orbit a dense positive nucleus, but no explanation of electron arrangement) led to Bohr's model (electrons travel in fixed energy levels/orbits, like planets around the sun). Then introduce the quantum mechanical model: electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals), not fixed paths. Use the analogy of a spinning fan blade — you know the region where the blade is, but not its exact position at any moment.

elaborate.description: Model comparison chart: Students complete a four-column chart (Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Quantum Mechanical) with rows for: key experiment, what it showed, model drawing, strengths, and limitations. Students write a paragraph explaining why the quantum model is considered the most accurate today.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) What unexpected result from the gold foil experiment led Rutherford to propose the nucleus? (2) How does the Bohr model differ from the Rutherford model? (3) Why is the quantum mechanical model described as a 'probability cloud' rather than fixed orbits?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the model comparison chart partially completed with Thomson's column filled in as an example; include sentence starters for the paragraph writing.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the data analysis and model comparison chart as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the contributions of Heisenberg (uncertainty principle) and Schrodinger (wave equation) to the quantum model and present a 1-minute explanation to the class.
differentiation.ell: Provide model comparison chart with labeled diagrams for each model; use a word bank for the paragraph writing; allow verbal exit ticket responses recorded on phone.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-drawn diagram of each model for labeling instead of drawing from scratch; break the exit ticket into three separate cards; allow use of the comparison chart during assessment.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American physicist whose experiments on beta decay contributed to our understanding of nuclear structure. Discuss how her work was overlooked for the Nobel Prize despite being essential to the discovery, connecting to issues of recognition and equity in science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who directed alpha particles at gold foil, discovered that the atom contains a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.' Students write similar appositive sentences for Bohr and Schrodinger.

vocabulary.definition: The small, dense, positively charged center of an atom containing protons and neutrons
A positively charged particle consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, used in Rutherford's gold foil experiment
A fixed region around the nucleus where electrons in the Bohr model are allowed to exist
A three-dimensional region around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron
The current model of the atom that describes electrons as existing in probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed circular paths
The lowest energy state of an atom, when all electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Rutherford's Gold Foil Experiment — Evidence for the Nucleus
Section 2: The Nuclear Model — Mostly Empty Space
Section 3: Bohr's Planetary Model — Electrons in Fixed Energy Levels
Section 4: The Quantum Mechanical Model — Probability Clouds and Orbitals
Section 5: Comparing All Four Atomic Models

cer.phenomenon: When Rutherford's team fired alpha particles at thin gold foil, 99% passed straight through, about 0.9% were deflected at small angles, and roughly 1 in 20,000 bounced straight back. Thomson's plum pudding model predicted that all particles would pass through with only slight deflections.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Rutherford's experimental results disprove the plum pudding model because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the specific percentages from the gold foil experiment data table to support your claim about atomic structure.
cer.reasoning_frame: If Thomson's model were correct, then___ because the positive charge would be spread evenly. However, the fact that some alpha particles bounced back means___, so Rutherford concluded that___.

lessons.title: Subatomic Particles, Atomic Number, and Mass Number
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom or ion using the atomic number and mass number.
lessons.circle_prompt: What makes you uniquely you? What is the one thing that, if it changed, would make you a completely different person?
lessons.do_now: Look at the periodic table entry for carbon: atomic number 6, atomic mass 12.01. What do you think these numbers tell us about the atom? Write two hypotheses.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Colored beads for modeling (red = proton, blue = neutron, yellow = electron, per group)

engage.description: Analogy: Show a photo of a stadium. The nucleus is like a marble on the 50-yard line — incredibly small but contains almost all the mass. The electrons are like mosquitoes buzzing around the upper decks. Ask: If the atom is mostly empty space, what gives matter its 'solidness'? (Introduce idea that electron repulsion creates the sensation of solidity.)

explore.description: Bead modeling: Using periodic tables, groups build models of five atoms (H, C, O, Na, Cl) with colored beads. For each, they count and record: protons (from atomic number), electrons (equals protons in a neutral atom), and neutrons (mass number minus atomic number). Students use whole-number mass numbers from the reference table. Groups then build Na+ and Cl- ions and note what changes.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes definitions: Atomic number = number of protons = identity of the element. Mass number = protons + neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons. In an ion, electrons differ from protons (cations lose electrons, anions gain). Work through examples on the board: What is the composition of Ca-40? Of S2-?

elaborate.description: Practice worksheet: Students complete a table for 10 atoms and ions, filling in element name, atomic number, mass number, number of protons, neutrons, electrons, and charge. Includes challenge items: an unknown element with 26 protons and 30 neutrons (iron-56), an ion with 10 electrons and 8 protons (O2-).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 17 electrons. Identify the element and give its mass number. (2) How does a sodium atom become a sodium ion? What changes and what stays the same? (3) Why does changing the number of protons change the element's identity?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled example row in the practice table; include a step-by-step formula card (protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number - atomic number; electrons = protons - charge).
differentiation.on_level: Complete bead modeling and practice worksheet as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research why the atomic mass on the periodic table is not a whole number (preview of isotopes and weighted averages) and explain in a short paragraph.
differentiation.ell: Provide the practice table with column headers translated; use color-coded formulas matching the bead colors; allow verbal explanation for the exit ticket.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice table to 6 items instead of 10; provide a calculator; allow use of the formula card during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Henry Moseley, the young British physicist who determined that atomic number (not atomic mass) defines an element. Moseley died at age 27 in World War I at Gallipoli — his loss led to policies protecting scientists from combat. Discuss how war and politics affect scientific progress.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'atomic number': The atomic number of an element is 8, so___. Carbon and nitrogen are next to each other on the periodic table, but___. Changing the number of protons changes the element's identity because___.

vocabulary.definition: A positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative mass of 1 amu
A neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative mass of 1 amu
A negatively charged subatomic particle found in orbitals outside the nucleus with negligible mass
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which determines the element's identity
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
An atom that has gained or lost electrons, giving it a net electrical charge

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Three Subatomic Particles — Location, Charge, and Mass
Section 2: Atomic Number — The Identity Card of an Element
Section 3: Mass Number and Calculating Neutrons
Section 4: Ions — When Atoms Gain or Lose Electrons

cer.phenomenon: A mystery atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, and 10 electrons. A second mystery atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, and 11 electrons. Are these the same element? Are they the same particle?
cer.claim_starter: I claim that these two particles are___ (the same / different) element(s) because___, but they differ in that___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the definitions of atomic number, mass number, and ion to compare the two particles systematically.
cer.reasoning_frame: Both particles have___ protons, which means they are both___ because atomic number determines___. However, particle 1 has___ electrons while particle 2 has___, so particle 1 is a___ because___.

lessons.title: Isotopes and Average Atomic Mass
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain what isotopes are and calculate the average atomic mass of an element from isotope data.
lessons.circle_prompt: Siblings share the same parents but can look very different. What makes siblings similar, and what makes each one unique?
lessons.do_now: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both carbon. What must be the same about them? What must be different? Use what you know about atomic number and mass number.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter
PS1.C: Nuclear Processes

materials: Isotope data cards (element, mass number, percent abundance) for 5 elements
Colored beads and bags for weighted average simulation

engage.description: Pose the question: The periodic table says chlorine's atomic mass is 35.45 amu. But no single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.45 — it is either 35 or 37. So where does 35.45 come from? Students discuss in pairs. Introduce the idea of a weighted average using a grade analogy: if homework is worth 20% and tests 80%, your average is weighted, not a simple mean.

explore.description: Bead bag simulation: Each group receives a bag containing a mix of two types of beads (e.g., 30 'light' beads at 2g each and 10 'heavy' beads at 3g each). Without knowing the contents, students count each type and calculate the percent abundance. Then they calculate the weighted average mass per bead. Reveal: this is exactly how average atomic mass works with isotopes.

explain.description: Define isotopes: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons (same atomic number, different mass number). Show how to calculate average atomic mass: sum of (mass of each isotope times its fractional abundance). Work through chlorine example: (34.97 x 0.7577) + (36.97 x 0.2423) = 35.45 amu. Discuss why the average is closer to 35 — because Cl-35 is more abundant.

elaborate.description: Practice problems: Students calculate average atomic mass for boron (2 isotopes), magnesium (3 isotopes), and silicon (3 isotopes) using provided data. Then reverse problem: Given that copper's average atomic mass is 63.55 and its two isotopes are Cu-63 (mass 62.93) and Cu-65 (mass 64.93), calculate the percent abundance of each.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Define isotope in terms of subatomic particles. (2) Silver has two isotopes: Ag-107 (51.84% abundance, mass 106.91) and Ag-109 (48.16% abundance, mass 108.90). Calculate the average atomic mass. (3) If an element's average atomic mass is 28.09 and is closest to mass number 28, what does this tell you about the most abundant isotope?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step calculation template: Step 1: Convert percent to decimal. Step 2: Multiply each isotope mass by its decimal abundance. Step 3: Add the products. Include a worked example next to each practice problem.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the bead simulation and calculation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Use mass spectrometry data (a real mass spectrum graph) to determine isotope masses and relative abundances, then calculate average atomic mass from the graph.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual calculation template with the formula written out in words; use color-coding to match each isotope to its contribution in the calculation.
differentiation.iep: Provide calculators and the formula on a reference card; reduce practice to 2 problems instead of 4; allow extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how Carbon-14 dating, discovered by Willard Libby, has been used to date artifacts from diverse civilizations — including the Dead Sea Scrolls, ancient Egyptian boats, and Indigenous Australian rock art. This technique relies on the predictable decay of a carbon isotope and has revolutionized archaeology worldwide.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'isotope': Isotopes of the same element have identical chemical properties because___. Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both carbon, but___. Chlorine-35 is more abundant than Chlorine-37, so the average atomic mass of chlorine is___.

vocabulary.definition: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, written as a superscript before the element symbol
The weighted average of the masses of all naturally occurring isotopes of an element
The percentage of a particular isotope found in a natural sample of an element
The unit used to express the mass of atoms and subatomic particles, defined as 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Are Isotopes? Same Element, Different Mass
Section 2: Isotope Notation — Reading and Writing
Section 3: Weighted Average — Why the Periodic Table Mass Is Not a Whole Number
Section 4: Calculating Average Atomic Mass from Isotope Data

cer.phenomenon: The periodic table lists the atomic mass of bromine as 79.90 amu. Bromine has two naturally occurring isotopes: Br-79 and Br-81. A student claims that since the average is almost exactly 80, the two isotopes must exist in equal amounts (50% each).
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's reasoning is___ (correct/incorrect) because the average atomic mass of 79.90 indicates___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the expected average if both isotopes were 50% abundant, then compare to the actual value of 79.90 to determine which isotope is more abundant.
cer.reasoning_frame: If both isotopes were equally abundant, the average would be___. Since the actual average is 79.90, which is closer to___, this means___ is more abundant because a weighted average is pulled toward the more common isotope.

lessons.title: Electron Configuration and Orbital Notation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write the full and shorthand electron configuration for elements 1-36 and represent them using orbital notation.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about where you sit in this school — your seat in this class, in lunch, on the bus. Why do you choose those spots? What rules or preferences guide you?
lessons.do_now: A hotel has floors numbered 1-4. Floor 1 has 1 room (holds 2 guests). Floor 2 has 4 rooms (holds 8 guests). Floor 3 has 4 rooms (holds 8 guests). If 11 guests check in, which floors fill first? Draw it out.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Orbital notation template (printed, with boxes for arrows)
Periodic table with electron configuration (1 per student)
Colored pencils (two colors for spin-up and spin-down electrons)

engage.description: Return to the neon sign anchoring phenomenon: Show images of different colored neon signs (red from neon, blue from argon, yellow from sodium). Ask: If every element emits different colors, the electrons in each element must be arranged differently. How are electrons arranged? Today we learn the rules.

explore.description: Guided discovery: Students use the periodic table to fill in an Aufbau diagram for the first 20 elements. They notice patterns: 1s fills first (2 electrons), then 2s (2), then 2p (6), then 3s (2), then 3p (6), then 4s (2). Teacher introduces the three rules: Aufbau principle (fill lowest energy first), Pauli exclusion principle (max 2 electrons per orbital, opposite spins), Hund's rule (one electron per orbital before pairing in a sublevel).

explain.description: Teacher demonstrates electron configuration notation (1s2 2s2 2p6...) and orbital notation (boxes with arrows) for nitrogen, sodium, and iron. Show the shorthand noble gas core notation: [Ne] 3s1 for sodium. Students practice writing configurations for 5 elements at their seats with guided feedback.

elaborate.description: Students complete configurations for 10 additional elements (Li through Kr) using both full notation and noble gas shorthand. Challenge: Identify the element given only its electron configuration (e.g., [Ar] 3d6 4s2 = iron). Students check answers using the periodic table as a self-checking tool.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the full electron configuration for phosphorus. (2) Write the noble gas shorthand for iron. (3) Draw the orbital notation for oxygen and explain why the 2p orbitals are filled the way they are (Hund's rule).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded Aufbau diagram with sublevel capacities pre-labeled; include a step-by-step guide: 'Step 1: Find the element's atomic number. Step 2: That is the total number of electrons. Step 3: Fill sublevels in order using the Aufbau diagram.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the electron configuration practice as designed with the Aufbau diagram as reference.
differentiation.advanced: Write electron configurations for ions (Fe2+, Fe3+, S2-) and explain why transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons when forming ions.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual Aufbau filling diagram with numbered steps and arrows showing the filling order; use color-coded orbital boxes; allow verbal explanation for Hund's rule question.
differentiation.iep: Reduce the number of practice elements from 10 to 5; provide a pre-drawn orbital notation template with labeled sublevels; allow use of the Aufbau diagram during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the development of quantum mechanics as a truly international effort: Niels Bohr (Denmark), Erwin Schrodinger (Austria), Werner Heisenberg (Germany), Satyendra Nath Bose (India), and Paul Dirac (England) all contributed to our understanding of electron behavior. Highlight Bose, whose work on quantum statistics with Einstein led to the 'boson' being named after him.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'electron configuration': Electrons fill the 2s sublevel before the 2p sublevel because___. Both oxygen and sulfur have 6 electrons in their outermost p sublevel, but___. The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill the lowest energy level first, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of electrons in the orbitals of an atom, written using sublevel notation (e.g., 1s2 2s2 2p3)
Electrons fill the lowest energy sublevel available before occupying higher energy sublevels
Each orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins
When filling orbitals of equal energy, electrons occupy each orbital singly before pairing up
A subdivision of an energy level designated as s, p, d, or f, each with a different number of orbitals
A shorthand for electron configuration that uses the previous noble gas symbol in brackets to represent filled inner shells

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Energy Levels, Sublevels, and Orbitals
Section 2: The Three Rules — Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund
Section 3: Writing Electron Configurations (Full Notation)
Section 4: Noble Gas Shorthand Notation
Section 5: Orbital Notation with Arrow Diagrams

cer.phenomenon: Nitrogen (Z=7) has an electron configuration of 1s2 2s2 2p3, with three unpaired electrons in its 2p orbitals. A student suggests that a more stable arrangement would be to pair two electrons in one 2p orbital and leave one 2p orbital empty, giving a configuration of 1s2 2s2 2p3 but with different orbital filling.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's proposed arrangement violates___ because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use Hund's rule and the concept of electron-electron repulsion to explain why nitrogen's actual orbital filling is more stable.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to Hund's rule, electrons in orbitals of equal energy will___ before___. This is because electrons are all negatively charged and___, so spreading out into separate orbitals minimizes___ and creates a more stable arrangement.

lessons.title: Electron Dot Structures and Valence Electrons
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can draw Lewis electron dot structures for main group elements and use valence electron count to predict an element's bonding behavior.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about your closest friend group. How many close friends do you keep in your inner circle? Why that number?
lessons.do_now: Write the electron configuration for sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl). How many electrons are in the outermost energy level of each? Circle those electrons — they are the key to chemical bonding.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

engage.description: Show students the Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb) and ask: What do all these elements have in common chemically? (They all react vigorously with water, they all form +1 ions.) Then show Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I): What do these have in common? (They all form -1 ions, they are all reactive nonmetals.) What determines these patterns? (The number of outermost electrons.)

explore.description: Students write electron configurations for one element from each main group (1-8) and identify the number of electrons in the outermost energy level. They record results in a table and look for the pattern: Group number = number of valence electrons for main group elements. Students then learn to draw Lewis dot structures by placing 1-8 dots around the element symbol following the pattern: one on each side before pairing.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the concept of valence electrons and their connection to the periodic table group number. Demonstrate Lewis dot structures for elements in each group. Key insight: elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties. Introduce the octet rule: atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve 8 valence electrons (2 for hydrogen/helium).

elaborate.description: Students draw Lewis dot structures for all elements in Period 2 and Period 3, then compare across periods. They predict: How many bonds will each element likely form? How many electrons will it gain or lose to achieve an octet? Students complete a prediction table for common elements (H, C, N, O, F, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Draw the Lewis dot structure for phosphorus and state how many valence electrons it has. (2) How many electrons does oxygen need to gain to achieve an octet? (3) Explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties using the concept of valence electrons.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a template with element symbols pre-written and the four sides labeled (top, right, bottom, left) for dot placement; include a 'Valence Electrons = Group Number' reference card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the Lewis dot practice and prediction table as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Draw Lewis dot structures for common ions and predict which elements will form stable compounds based on complementary valence electron needs (e.g., Na donates 1, Cl accepts 1).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual step-by-step guide for drawing Lewis dots with numbered steps and example drawings; use the periodic table color-coded by group to reinforce the group number pattern.
differentiation.iep: Reduce the prediction table to 6 elements instead of 12; provide a completed example row; allow use of periodic table and reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Gilbert N. Lewis, who developed the dot notation system in 1916. Despite being nominated 41 times, Lewis never won the Nobel Prize — sparking discussion about how recognition in science can be influenced by personal rivalries (his conflict with Nernst) and institutional politics.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'valence electrons': Sodium has one valence electron, so it tends to___. Fluorine and chlorine both have 7 valence electrons because___. Neon has 8 valence electrons and is extremely stable, but sodium has only 1, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The electrons in the outermost energy level of an atom that participate in chemical bonding
A diagram that shows the valence electrons of an atom as dots arranged around the element symbol
The tendency of atoms to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a full set of 8 valence electrons
The inner electrons of an atom that are not in the outermost energy level and do not participate in bonding
An arrangement with a full outermost energy level, like the noble gases, which makes an atom unreactive

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Valence Electrons — The Outermost Electrons
Section 2: Connecting Valence Electrons to the Periodic Table Group Number
Section 3: Drawing Lewis Electron Dot Structures
Section 4: The Octet Rule — Why 8 Is the Magic Number
Section 5: Predicting Bonding Behavior from Valence Electrons

cer.phenomenon: Lithium (Group 1), sodium (Group 1), and potassium (Group 1) all react vigorously with water, producing hydrogen gas and a basic solution. Meanwhile, helium (Group 18), neon (Group 18), and argon (Group 18) do not react with anything under normal conditions.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the difference in reactivity between Group 1 and Group 18 elements is due to___.
cer.evidence_source: Draw Lewis dot structures for one element from each group and compare the number of valence electrons to the octet rule.
cer.reasoning_frame: Group 1 elements have___ valence electron(s), which means they need to___ to achieve a stable octet. This makes them___ because___. Group 18 elements already have___, so they___ because___.

lessons.title: Periodic Table Organization and Periodic Trends
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how elements are organized on the periodic table and predict trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity across periods and down groups.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about how your family organizes something at home — spices, tools, clothes. What is the organizing principle? Could it be organized differently?
lessons.do_now: Look at the first 20 elements on the periodic table. List three patterns you notice in how they are arranged. Consider: What increases left to right? What changes as you go down a group?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Periodic table (large wall poster and individual copies)
Periodic trends data set (atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity for first 36 elements)

engage.description: Show students Mendeleev's original periodic table (1869) and the modern periodic table side by side. Mendeleev organized by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. He predicted the properties of 'eka-silicon' (germanium) with remarkable accuracy. Ask: How did organizing elements reveal patterns that allowed predictions?

explore.description: Data analysis and graphing: Students plot two graphs using provided data. Graph 1: Atomic radius (in pm) vs. atomic number for elements 1-36 (line graph). Graph 2: First ionization energy (in kJ/mol) vs. atomic number for elements 1-36. Students color-code each period on their graphs. In pairs, they answer: What happens to atomic radius across a period? Down a group? What happens to ionization energy across a period? Down a group?

explain.description: Teacher explains the trends using electron structure. Atomic radius decreases across a period because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer (same energy level, more protons). Atomic radius increases down a group because new energy levels are added. Ionization energy increases across a period (harder to remove an electron from a smaller atom with more nuclear charge) and decreases down a group (outermost electron is farther from the nucleus). Introduce electronegativity as the atom's ability to attract bonding electrons — follows the same trend as ionization energy.

elaborate.description: Students create a periodic trends foldable: three flaps labeled Atomic Radius, Ionization Energy, and Electronegativity. Under each flap, they draw arrows showing the trend direction across periods and down groups, write a one-sentence explanation, and give a specific example comparison (e.g., 'Na has a larger atomic radius than Cl because...').

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Rank these elements by atomic radius from smallest to largest: Na, Mg, Al, K. Explain your reasoning. (2) Which has a higher ionization energy, oxygen or sulfur? Why? (3) Why does electronegativity generally increase from left to right across a period?

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-scaled graph axes with data points partially plotted; include a trends summary card with arrows and one-sentence explanations for reference during the foldable activity.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the graphing, analysis, and foldable as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Identify and explain exceptions to the general trends (e.g., why does ionization energy dip from Be to B, or from N to O?) using sublevel electron configuration.
differentiation.ell: Provide graphing instructions with numbered visual steps; use a bilingual trends summary with diagrams showing 'bigger/smaller' arrows; sentence frames for the foldable explanations.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-made graphs that students analyze (rather than creating from scratch); reduce foldable to two trends instead of three; allow extended time for exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Dmitri Mendeleev (Russia), Julius Lothar Meyer (Germany), and John Newlands (England) — three scientists who independently recognized periodic patterns around the same time. Highlight how scientific discoveries often emerge simultaneously across cultures when the foundational knowledge is ripe, challenging the 'lone genius' narrative.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'atomic radius': Atomic radius decreases across a period because___. Potassium is in the same group as sodium, but it has a larger atomic radius because___. Fluorine has a very small atomic radius and high electronegativity, so___.

vocabulary.definition: Half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element
The energy required to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state
A measure of an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond
A horizontal row on the periodic table; elements in the same period have the same number of energy levels
A vertical column on the periodic table; elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties
The tendency of an element to lose electrons and exhibit properties of metals (luster, conductivity, malleability)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Organization of the Periodic Table — Periods and Groups
Section 2: Atomic Radius Trend — Across Periods and Down Groups
Section 3: Ionization Energy Trend — Why It Takes More Energy Across a Period
Section 4: Electronegativity Trend — The Pull on Bonding Electrons
Section 5: Metallic Character and Its Relationship to Other Trends

cer.phenomenon: A student examines data showing that lithium (Li) has an atomic radius of 152 pm, while fluorine (F), in the same period, has an atomic radius of only 64 pm. Both elements are in Period 2. The student claims that fluorine is smaller because it has fewer electrons.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's explanation is incorrect because fluorine actually has___ electrons than lithium. The real reason fluorine has a smaller atomic radius is___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the atomic number, electron configuration, and nuclear charge of lithium and fluorine to explain the trend in atomic radius across Period 2.
cer.reasoning_frame: As we move from Li to F across Period 2, the number of protons increases from___ to___, but electrons are added to the same energy level. This means the nuclear charge___ while the shielding___, so the electrons are pulled___, resulting in a___ atomic radius.

lessons.title: Metals, Nonmetals, Metalloids, and Element Families
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify elements as metals, nonmetals, or metalloids and describe the characteristic properties and common reactions of the major element families.
lessons.circle_prompt: Every family has its quirks and shared traits. If elements are grouped into families, what 'family traits' might they share?
lessons.do_now: Pick up the three samples on your desk (a piece of copper wire, a piece of sulfur, and a silicon chip). Describe each one: Is it shiny or dull? Bendable or brittle? Which might conduct electricity?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Element sample set per group (copper, iron, aluminum, sulfur, carbon, silicon if available)
Malleability testing tools (small hammer, anvil surface)
Element family reference cards (Alkali metals, Alkaline earth, Halogens, Noble gases)

engage.description: Show images of everyday objects: a copper pipe, a diamond ring, a silicon computer chip, a helium balloon, aluminum foil. Ask: What do the elements in these objects have in common, and what makes them different? How does the periodic table help us predict which elements behave similarly?

explore.description: Property testing stations: Groups test 4-6 element samples for luster (shiny vs. dull), malleability (bendable vs. brittle), and conductivity (using a circuit tester). They record results in a data table and attempt to classify each element as metal, nonmetal, or metalloid based on their observations.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the metal/nonmetal/metalloid classification and locates the staircase line on the periodic table. Review properties of each category. Then introduce the major element families: Alkali metals (Group 1 — soft, reactive, form +1 ions), Alkaline earth metals (Group 2 — form +2 ions), Halogens (Group 17 — reactive nonmetals, form -1 ions), Noble gases (Group 18 — full valence shell, unreactive). Connect family properties to valence electron count.

elaborate.description: Element family poster activity: Each group is assigned one element family. They create a mini-poster with: family name and group number, number of valence electrons, 3 common elements and their uses, key physical and chemical properties, and a real-world application. Groups present in 1 minute each.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) A mystery element is shiny, conducts electricity, but is brittle. Is it most likely a metal, nonmetal, or metalloid? Explain. (2) Why are alkali metals stored in oil? (3) Explain why noble gases are chemically unreactive using the concept of valence electrons.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed data table with property categories pre-listed and a metal/nonmetal/metalloid decision guide (If shiny AND conductive AND malleable, then = metal).
differentiation.on_level: Complete property testing and element family poster as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research transition metals and explain why they can form multiple ions (variable oxidation states due to d-electron involvement); present one example with electron configurations.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual properties chart with photographs showing luster/dull, bendable/brittle; bilingual element family cards; allow poster to include diagrams instead of written descriptions.
differentiation.iep: Pair with a partner for property testing; provide a simplified poster template with fill-in sections; allow verbal presentation instead of written.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the elements in your smartphone come from around the world: cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo (raising ethical mining concerns), lithium from Chile and Australia, rare earth elements from China. Connect the periodic table to global supply chains, labor practices, and environmental justice in mining communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'The alkali metals, a group of highly reactive elements in Group 1 of the periodic table, all have one valence electron and react vigorously with water.' Students write appositive sentences for halogens and noble gases.

vocabulary.definition: An element that is typically shiny, malleable, ductile, and a good conductor of heat and electricity; metals tend to lose electrons to form positive ions
An element that is typically dull, brittle, and a poor conductor; nonmetals tend to gain electrons to form negative ions
An element with properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals, often used as semiconductors
A Group 1 element (excluding hydrogen) that is soft, highly reactive, and forms +1 ions
A Group 17 element that is a highly reactive nonmetal and forms -1 ions
A Group 18 element with a full valence shell that is chemically unreactive under normal conditions

Section 2: The Alkali Metals (Group 1) and Alkaline Earth Metals (Group 2)
Section 3: The Halogens (Group 17) and Noble Gases (Group 18)
Section 4: Transition Metals — The Middle of the Table
