cer.phenomenon: Silicon is located on the staircase line of the periodic table. It has a shiny appearance like a metal but is brittle like a nonmetal. It conducts electricity, but not as well as copper. Silicon is the basis of all modern computer chips.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that silicon is classified as a metalloid because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the property data from the Explore activity and compare silicon's characteristics to the defining properties of metals and nonmetals.
cer.reasoning_frame: Silicon shares some properties with metals, such as___, but also shares properties with nonmetals, such as___. Its intermediate conductivity makes it a___, which is why it is useful as a___ in electronics because___.

lessons.title: Introduction to Nuclear Chemistry: Radioactive Decay
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe the three main types of radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) and write balanced nuclear equations showing changes in atomic number and mass number.
lessons.circle_prompt: Some things last almost forever, and some things break down quickly. What is something in your life that changed or decayed over time? How did you notice it happening?
lessons.do_now: Carbon-14 is an isotope used to date ancient artifacts. It slowly transforms into Nitrogen-14 over thousands of years. What must be changing inside the atom for carbon to become nitrogen? (Hint: What defines an element?)

dci: PS1.C: Nuclear Processes

materials: Nuclear decay reference card (alpha, beta, gamma — symbol, mass, charge, penetrating power)
Radioactive decay simulation (pennies or M&Ms for half-life activity — 100 per group)

engage.description: Show images of the Chernobyl exclusion zone — abandoned buildings, overgrown vegetation, the concrete sarcophagus. Ask: Why is this area still uninhabitable 40 years later? What is radioactivity, and why do some materials remain dangerous for thousands of years while others become safe quickly? Introduce the idea that some atomic nuclei are unstable and release energy and particles to become more stable.

explore.description: Half-life penny simulation: Each group starts with 100 pennies (representing radioactive atoms) in a box. Shake and pour — remove all 'heads' (decayed atoms). Count remaining 'tails' and record. Repeat for 8 rounds. Students graph the number of remaining atoms vs. trial number. Class discusses: What pattern do you see? (exponential decay) How many trials does it take to reach half? (approximately 1 trial = 1 half-life)

explain.description: Teacher introduces the three types of radioactive decay. Alpha decay: nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2. Beta decay: a neutron converts to a proton and emits an electron, mass number stays the same, atomic number increases by 1. Gamma radiation: energy emission only, no change in mass or atomic number. Demonstrate writing balanced nuclear equations for each type. Show penetrating power comparison: alpha stopped by paper, beta by aluminum, gamma by lead.

elaborate.description: Practice problems: Students write balanced nuclear equations for 6 decay reactions (2 alpha, 2 beta, 2 mixed). For each, they identify the parent isotope, the daughter isotope, and the type of radiation emitted. Challenge: Given that U-238 undergoes alpha decay to Th-234, which then undergoes beta decay, write both equations and identify the final product.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of Ra-226. (2) In beta decay, what happens inside the nucleus? (3) A radioactive sample has a half-life of 10 years. If you start with 200 g, how much remains after 30 years?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a nuclear equation template showing where to place mass numbers and atomic numbers; include a step-by-step checklist: 'Step 1: Write the parent isotope. Step 2: Write the decay particle. Step 3: Calculate the missing mass number and atomic number. Step 4: Look up the new element.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the half-life simulation and nuclear equation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the concept of decay chains (e.g., U-238 decay series to Pb-206) and create a diagram showing the full sequence of alpha and beta decays.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual reference card with diagrams of each decay type showing particle emission with bilingual labels; use color-coding for mass number (red) and atomic number (blue) in equations.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems from 6 to 3; provide a periodic table with atomic numbers clearly labeled; allow use of reference card during exit ticket; pair with a partner for the penny simulation.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Marie Curie (Polish-French physicist) and her daughter Irene Joliot-Curie — the only mother-daughter Nobel laureates. Both made groundbreaking discoveries in radioactivity. Also discuss the disproportionate impact of nuclear testing on indigenous communities: the Marshall Islands, Navajo uranium miners, and Aboriginal Australians near Maralinga. Connect to environmental justice and the legacy of nuclear science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'radioactive decay': Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay because___. Alpha and beta radiation both involve particle emission, but___. The atomic number changes during alpha and beta decay, so the element's identity___.

vocabulary.definition: The spontaneous emission of particles or energy from an unstable nucleus to become more stable
A type of nuclear decay in which the nucleus emits an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons), decreasing mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2
A type of nuclear decay in which a neutron converts to a proton and emits a high-speed electron, increasing atomic number by 1 with no change in mass number
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus during decay; has no mass or charge
The time required for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay
An equation showing a nuclear reaction, where the sum of mass numbers and atomic numbers must be balanced on both sides

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why Are Some Nuclei Unstable? — Nuclear Stability
Section 2: Alpha Decay — Emission of a Helium Nucleus
Section 3: Beta Decay — Neutron to Proton Conversion
Section 4: Gamma Radiation — Energy Without Particles
Section 5: Half-Life and Radioactive Decay Curves

cer.phenomenon: Archaeologists discover two wooden artifacts at the same site. Artifact A contains 25% of its original Carbon-14, while Artifact B contains 50% of its original Carbon-14. The half-life of Carbon-14 is approximately 5,730 years.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Artifact A is approximately___ years old and Artifact B is approximately___ years old because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the half-life definition and the percentage of remaining Carbon-14 to calculate the number of half-lives that have passed for each artifact.
cer.reasoning_frame: Artifact B has 50% remaining, which means___ half-life(s) have passed, so it is approximately___ years old. Artifact A has 25% remaining, which means___ half-lives have passed (50% then 25%), so it is approximately___ years old. This demonstrates that___ because___.

units.title: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Table salt (NaCl) melts at 801 degrees C and dissolves easily in water, while diamond (pure carbon) melts at over 3,500 degrees C and does not dissolve in anything. Both are crystalline solids. Why do substances made of atoms behave so differently?
essential_questions: How do atoms bond together, and what determines the type of bond that forms?
How does the three-dimensional shape of a molecule affect its properties?
Why do some substances have high melting points while others are gases at room temperature?
units.crse_theme: Students explore the chemistry of materials in everyday life across cultures — from the ionic compounds in traditional African salt mining to the molecular structures of natural dyes used by indigenous peoples. The unit connects particulate-level bonding to the bulk properties of culturally significant materials.

summative: Bonding and Molecular Structure Lab Practical
Unit 3 Exam: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure

investigations: Investigation 4: Comparing Properties of Ionic and Molecular Compounds
Investigation 5: Determining Molecular Polarity from Molecular Geometry

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how ionic bonds form through electron transfer between metals and nonmetals and describe the structure and properties of ionic compounds.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you gave something to someone because they needed it more than you. How did it change both of you?
lessons.do_now: Draw the Lewis dot structures for sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl). Sodium has 1 valence electron and chlorine has 7. How could both atoms end up with 8 valence electrons? Sketch your idea.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Ionic compound sample set: NaCl, CaCO3, MgSO4 (Epsom salt)
Beakers with distilled water for dissolving tests
Crystal lattice model (NaCl, physical or digital 3D model)

engage.description: Demo: Dissolve table salt in water and test conductivity — the bulb lights up. Then test solid salt — no conductivity. Then test sugar water — no conductivity. Ask: Why does salt conduct only when dissolved? What is special about salt at the particle level that sugar does not have? Record student hypotheses.

explore.description: Students draw step-by-step diagrams of ionic bond formation for NaCl: (1) Lewis dot structures of separate Na and Cl atoms, (2) arrow showing electron transfer from Na to Cl, (3) resulting Na+ and Cl- ions with brackets and charges, (4) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Then repeat for MgCl2 (Mg gives 2 electrons, one to each Cl). Students discuss in pairs: Why does Mg form +2 while Na forms +1?

explain.description: Teacher formalizes ionic bonding: metals lose electrons (form cations), nonmetals gain electrons (form anions), oppositely charged ions attract in a 3D crystal lattice. Show the NaCl crystal lattice model — each Na+ is surrounded by 6 Cl- and vice versa. Connect structure to properties: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice), brittleness (shifting layers causes like charges to align and repel), conductivity when dissolved or melted (ions are free to move).

elaborate.description: Property prediction: Given three unknown ionic compounds with melting point data (compound X: 770 C, compound Y: 2570 C, compound Z: 1418 C), students predict which has the strongest ionic bonds. Then students explain why ionic compounds dissolve in water but not in oil, using the concept of polar water molecules surrounding ions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Draw the ionic bond formation between calcium (Ca) and fluorine (F), showing electron transfer and resulting ions. (2) Explain why NaCl has a high melting point using the crystal lattice model. (3) Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity, but dissolved NaCl does?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed ionic bonding diagram with the Lewis structures pre-drawn; students only need to show the electron transfer and write the ion charges. Include a step-by-step guide for predicting ion charges from group number.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ionic bonding diagrams and property analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on lattice energy — how the size and charge of ions affect the strength of the ionic bond (e.g., compare NaCl to MgO lattice energies and explain the difference).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual glossary with diagrams of electron transfer labeled in English and Spanish; use color-coded ion charges (red for positive, blue for negative) throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Chunked worksheet with one ionic bond per page; provide a periodic table with ion charges clearly marked for common elements; extended time for exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the historical significance of salt across cultures: Roman soldiers were partially paid in salt (origin of 'salary'), salt mining in Timbuktu was central to West African trade empires, and Gandhi's Salt March (1930) was a pivotal act of civil disobedience against British rule in India. All of this over NaCl — an ionic compound.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'ionic compound': Ionic compounds have high melting points because___. Ionic compounds conduct electricity in solution, but not as solids, because___. Sodium loses one electron to form Na+, so chlorine___.

vocabulary.definition: A bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, resulting from the transfer of electrons from a metal to a nonmetal
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons
A repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic compound, held together by electrostatic forces
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles
The process by which one or more electrons move from a metal atom to a nonmetal atom during ionic bond formation

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: How Ionic Bonds Form — Electron Transfer
Section 2: Drawing Ionic Bond Diagrams
Section 3: Crystal Lattice Structure — 3D Arrangement of Ions
Section 4: Properties of Ionic Compounds (Melting Point, Conductivity, Solubility, Brittleness)

cer.phenomenon: A student tests two white crystalline substances. Substance A melts at 801 degrees C, dissolves in water, and the solution conducts electricity. Substance B melts at 186 degrees C, dissolves in water, but the solution does not conduct electricity.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Substance A is an ionic compound and Substance B is a molecular compound because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the melting point, solubility, and conductivity data for both substances to the expected properties of ionic and molecular compounds.
cer.reasoning_frame: Substance A has a high melting point because___, and its solution conducts electricity because___. Substance B has a low melting point because___, and its solution does not conduct because___, indicating it is made of___.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how covalent bonds form through electron sharing and draw accurate Lewis structures for simple molecular compounds.
lessons.circle_prompt: When is sharing better than giving something away completely? Can you think of a situation where sharing made both sides better off?
lessons.do_now: Two hydrogen atoms each have 1 valence electron and need 2 to be stable. Neither wants to completely give up its electron. How could both atoms get a full outer shell? Sketch your idea.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
Bond type spectrum diagram (nonpolar covalent — polar covalent — ionic)

engage.description: Show two images: NaCl crystal (ionic) and H2O molecule (covalent). Ask: In NaCl, electrons are transferred. But in water, hydrogen and oxygen share electrons. Why would two nonmetals share rather than transfer? Introduce the concept: when two atoms have similar electronegativity, neither can pull electrons away completely, so they share.

explore.description: Guided Lewis structure construction: Teacher demonstrates the step-by-step process for drawing Lewis structures: (1) count total valence electrons, (2) draw the skeletal structure with single bonds, (3) complete octets on outer atoms, (4) place remaining electrons on the central atom, (5) convert lone pairs to multiple bonds if the central atom lacks an octet. Students practice with H2, O2, N2, H2O, CO2, and NH3, checking each with molecular model kits.

explain.description: Teacher explains single, double, and triple bonds as sharing 2, 4, or 6 electrons respectively. Distinguish between bonding pairs and lone pairs. Introduce the concept of bond strength and length: triple bonds are shortest and strongest, single bonds are longest and weakest. Discuss the difference between molecular covalent substances (discrete molecules like H2O) and network covalent substances (continuous lattice like diamond or SiO2).

elaborate.description: Students draw Lewis structures for 6 additional molecules: HCl, CCl4, CH4, C2H4 (has a double bond), HCN (has a triple bond), and PCl3. For each, they identify the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs. Challenge: Why does PCl3 have a lone pair on phosphorus while CCl4 does not?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Draw the Lewis structure for carbon dioxide (CO2) and identify the type of bonds present. (2) How many total valence electrons are in a molecule of ammonia (NH3)? Draw its Lewis structure. (3) Explain why two oxygen atoms form a double bond rather than a single bond.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Lewis structure checklist card: Step 1 — count valence electrons (use periodic table), Step 2 — draw skeleton, etc. Include a worked example (HCl) at the top of the practice sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete Lewis structure practice and model building as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Draw Lewis structures for molecules with expanded octets (SF6, PCl5) and explain why elements in Period 3 and beyond can exceed the octet rule.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual step-by-step Lewis structure guide with numbered diagrams; allow students to use molecular model kits to verify structures before drawing.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice molecules from 6 to 4; provide a valence electron reference card; allow use of molecular model kits during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Linus Pauling, one of only two people to win two unshared Nobel Prizes (Chemistry and Peace). His work on the nature of the chemical bond revolutionized our understanding of covalent bonding. Also discuss his later controversial advocacy for vitamin C megadoses — showing that even brilliant scientists can hold views not supported by evidence outside their expertise.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'covalent bond': Two oxygen atoms form a double bond because___. Both ionic and covalent bonds involve valence electrons, but___. Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its octet, so it forms___.

vocabulary.definition: A bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
A covalent bond in which one pair of electrons is shared between two atoms
A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms
A covalent bond in which three pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms
A pair of valence electrons that is not shared between atoms and belongs to only one atom
A pair of electrons shared between two atoms in a covalent bond
A diagram showing all valence electrons in a molecule as dots or lines between atoms

Section 2: Steps for Drawing Lewis Structures
Section 3: Single, Double, and Triple Bonds
Section 4: Bonding Pairs vs. Lone Pairs
Section 5: Molecular vs. Network Covalent Substances

cer.phenomenon: Nitrogen gas (N2) makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere and is extremely unreactive under normal conditions. However, at high temperatures and pressures (like in a car engine or during lightning), nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides (NOx), which are pollutants.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that nitrogen gas is unreactive under normal conditions because of the type of covalent bond between its atoms, which is a___.
cer.evidence_source: Draw the Lewis structure of N2, identify the bond type, and compare its bond energy to that of single and double bonds.
cer.reasoning_frame: N2 has a___ bond, which requires approximately 945 kJ/mol of energy to break. This is much more than a single bond (~160 kJ/mol) because___. Under normal conditions, this energy is not available, so N2 remains stable. However, at high temperatures___.

lessons.title: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe the sea of electrons model of metallic bonding and compare the properties of ionic, covalent, and metallic substances based on their bonding type.
lessons.circle_prompt: In a team sport or group project, when does it work best for everyone to contribute equally rather than having set roles? How is that different from assigned positions?
lessons.do_now: A copper wire conducts electricity as a solid, bends without breaking, and is shiny. NaCl is brittle and only conducts when dissolved. What is different about the bonding in copper vs. NaCl that explains these differences?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Metal samples: copper wire, aluminum foil, iron nail
Property cards for sorting activity (15 cards with properties)

engage.description: Demo: Bend a copper wire back and forth (malleable). Hit an NaCl crystal with a hammer (it shatters). Ask: Copper atoms and Na/Cl ions are both arranged in crystal lattices. Why does copper bend while NaCl shatters? Students discuss and predict.

explore.description: Students test metal samples for conductivity (as solids), malleability (bending), and luster. They record observations and compare to their previous data on ionic and covalent compounds. Then students examine the 'sea of electrons' model diagram: metal cations are arranged in a lattice, surrounded by delocalized valence electrons that flow freely.

explain.description: Teacher explains metallic bonding: metal atoms release their valence electrons into a shared 'sea' that holds the cations together. This delocalized electron cloud explains: conductivity (electrons flow freely), malleability/ductility (layers of cations can slide without breaking bonds because the electron sea reshapes around them), luster (free electrons absorb and re-emit light). Build a comprehensive comparison table: ionic (electron transfer, high MP, brittle, conducts when dissolved), covalent (electron sharing, low MP, nonconductor), metallic (delocalized electrons, variable MP, malleable, conducts as solid).

elaborate.description: Property sorting card activity: Students receive 15 cards with properties (e.g., 'conducts as a solid,' 'brittle,' 'low melting point,' 'forms a crystal lattice with delocalized electrons') and sort them into three columns: ionic, covalent, and metallic. Some properties may fit more than one category — students must justify their placement.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A mystery substance is shiny, conducts electricity as a solid, has a high melting point, and is malleable. (1) What type of bonding does it have? (2) Describe the bonding model. (3) If this substance were ionic instead, which property would change, and how?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the comparison table partially completed with ionic column filled in; include a visual diagram of each bonding model with labeled key features for reference during the sorting activity.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the property testing, comparison table, and sorting activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on metallic bonding in alloys — how mixing different metals (bronze, steel, brass) changes properties, and explain at the atomic level why alloys are often harder than pure metals.
differentiation.ell: Provide property sorting cards with diagrams alongside text descriptions; include a bilingual comparison chart with visual icons for each property (flame icon for high MP, lightning bolt for conductivity).
differentiation.iep: Reduce sorting cards from 15 to 10; provide a reference sheet with the three bonding models side by side; allow partner work for the sorting activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the history of metallurgy across civilizations: ancient Egyptians used bronze (alloy of copper and tin), the Hittites pioneered iron smelting, West African kingdoms independently developed iron working by 1000 BCE, and Japanese swordsmiths created legendary steel through careful temperature control. Metallic bonding knowledge is the foundation of materials science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'metallic bonding': Metals are good conductors of electricity because___. Both metallic and ionic substances form crystal lattices, but metals are malleable while ionic compounds are brittle because___. The valence electrons in a metal are delocalized, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A bond formed by the attraction between metal cations and a surrounding sea of delocalized electrons
Valence electrons in a metallic bond that are free to move throughout the entire metal structure rather than being attached to individual atoms
The ability of a material to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without breaking
The ability of a material to be drawn into thin wires without breaking
A mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a nonmetal, that has metallic properties

Section 2: Properties of Metals Explained by Metallic Bonding
Section 3: Comparing Ionic, Covalent, and Metallic Bonds
Section 4: Bond Type and Bulk Properties — Connecting Structure to Function

cer.phenomenon: Copper is used for electrical wiring in homes. Sodium chloride is used to de-ice roads in winter. Sugar (C12H22O11) is used to sweeten food. Each substance serves a different purpose because of its unique properties, which are determined by its bonding.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that copper is used for wiring because of its___ bonding, NaCl de-ices roads because of its___ bonding, and sugar dissolves easily because of its___ bonding.
cer.evidence_source: For each substance, identify the bond type, describe the bonding model, and connect it to the specific property that makes it useful for its purpose.
cer.reasoning_frame: Copper's metallic bonding means it has___, which is essential for wiring because___. NaCl's ionic bonding means it___ when dissolved in water, which lowers the freezing point because___. Sugar's covalent bonding means it___, so___.

lessons.title: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can predict the three-dimensional shape of a molecule using VSEPR theory and the number of bonding and lone pairs around the central atom.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to arrange 4 balloons tied together at a central point so they were as far apart as possible, what shape would they make? What about 3 balloons? 2?
lessons.do_now: Draw the Lewis structure for water (H2O) and methane (CH4). Count the number of electron groups (bonding pairs + lone pairs) around the central atom in each. Predict: Will these molecules be the same shape? Why or why not?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter
PS2.B: Types of Interactions

materials: Balloon sets (4-6 per group for geometry modeling)
Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
3D molecular geometry posters or digital models

engage.description: Balloon demo: Inflate 4 balloons and tie them together at a central point. Ask: What shape do they naturally form? (tetrahedral) Why? (They repel each other and maximize the space between them.) Now pop one balloon — what shape do the remaining 3 form? (trigonal pyramidal) This is exactly how electron pairs around a central atom determine molecular shape.

explore.description: Students use molecular model kits to build five molecules: BeCl2 (2 bonding pairs, linear), BF3 (3 bonding pairs, trigonal planar), CH4 (4 bonding pairs, tetrahedral), NH3 (3 bonding + 1 lone pair, trigonal pyramidal), H2O (2 bonding + 2 lone pairs, bent). For each, they record: Lewis structure, number of bonding pairs, number of lone pairs, 3D shape name, and approximate bond angle.

explain.description: Teacher introduces VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory: electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Key shapes and angles: linear (180 degrees), trigonal planar (120 degrees), tetrahedral (109.5 degrees), trigonal pyramidal (~107 degrees), bent (~104.5 degrees). Emphasize that lone pairs take up more space than bonding pairs, so they compress bond angles.

elaborate.description: Students predict the molecular geometry for 6 additional molecules by drawing Lewis structures first, then counting electron groups: CO2, SO2, CCl4, PCl3, H2S, and CHCl3. They build each with model kits to verify their predictions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Draw the Lewis structure for ammonia (NH3) and name its molecular geometry. (2) Explain why H2O is bent even though oxygen has 4 electron groups. (3) Predict the shape of CO2 and explain why it is different from H2O, even though both have 2 atoms bonded to a central atom.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a VSEPR decision flowchart: 'How many electron groups? -> How many are lone pairs? -> Shape name and angle.' Include model kit building instructions with photographs for each shape.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the model building and geometry predictions as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Extend to 5 and 6 electron group geometries (trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral) and predict shapes for SF4, ClF3, and XeF2.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual VSEPR chart with 3D photographs of each geometry labeled in English and native language; allow students to take photos of their model kit structures as evidence.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice molecules from 6 to 4; provide a completed Lewis structure for each molecule so students focus only on geometry prediction; allow use of model kits during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding molecular geometry is critical in pharmaceutical chemistry — the shape of a drug molecule determines whether it can fit into a receptor in the body (like a key in a lock). Highlight Tu Youyou, the Chinese chemist who won the Nobel Prize for discovering artemisinin, an antimalarial drug, by studying traditional Chinese herbal medicine and understanding the molecular structure of the active compound.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'molecular geometry': Water has a bent shape because___. Both CH4 and NH3 have four electron groups around the central atom, but their molecular shapes are different because___. Lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly, so the bond angle in NH3 is___.

vocabulary.definition: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory — a model that predicts molecular geometry based on the idea that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange to be as far apart as possible
The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule
A molecular shape with 2 bonding groups and no lone pairs, forming a 180-degree bond angle
A molecular shape with 4 bonding groups and no lone pairs, forming 109.5-degree bond angles
A molecular shape with 3 bonding groups and 1 lone pair, forming approximately 107-degree bond angles
A molecular shape with 2 bonding groups and 1 or 2 lone pairs, forming bond angles less than 120 or 109.5 degrees

Section 2: Counting Electron Groups (Bonding Pairs and Lone Pairs)
Section 3: Five Key Molecular Geometries and Their Bond Angles
Section 4: How Lone Pairs Affect Molecular Shape
Section 5: Predicting Geometry from Lewis Structures

cer.phenomenon: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a linear molecule with a 180-degree bond angle, while water (H2O) is a bent molecule with a 104.5-degree bond angle. Both molecules have a central atom bonded to two other atoms, yet their shapes are completely different.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that CO2 and H2O have different molecular geometries because___.
cer.evidence_source: Draw Lewis structures for both molecules, count bonding pairs and lone pairs around each central atom, and apply VSEPR theory to determine the expected geometry.
cer.reasoning_frame: CO2 has___ bonding pairs and___ lone pairs around carbon, so VSEPR predicts a___ shape. H2O has___ bonding pairs and___ lone pairs around oxygen, so VSEPR predicts a___ shape. The lone pairs on oxygen___ the bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle to___.

lessons.title: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can determine whether a bond is polar or nonpolar using electronegativity differences and predict whether a molecule is polar or nonpolar based on its geometry.
lessons.circle_prompt: In a tug-of-war, what happens when both sides pull equally? What happens when one side is much stronger?
lessons.do_now: Use the electronegativity values on your reference table to find the difference between: (a) H and Cl, (b) Na and Cl, (c) Cl and Cl. Which pair shares most equally? Which pair has the biggest difference?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Charged rod and water stream demonstration materials (plastic rod, fur, buret with water)

engage.description: Demo: Run a thin stream of water from a buret. Bring a charged plastic rod near the stream — the water bends toward the rod. Repeat with hexane — no bending. Ask: Why does water respond to the charged rod but hexane does not? Both are clear liquids. The answer lies in molecular polarity.

explore.description: Students calculate electronegativity differences for 10 atom pairs and classify each bond as nonpolar covalent (0-0.4), polar covalent (0.4-1.7), or ionic (>1.7). They draw arrows on bond diagrams pointing from the less electronegative atom to the more electronegative atom (dipole arrows). Then they examine 4 molecules (CO2, H2O, CCl4, HCl) and draw dipole arrows for each bond.

explain.description: Teacher explains the two-step process for determining molecular polarity: (1) Are the individual bonds polar? (Use electronegativity difference.) (2) Does the molecular geometry cause the dipoles to cancel or reinforce? Symmetric molecules (CO2, CCl4) have polar bonds that cancel — the molecule is nonpolar. Asymmetric molecules (H2O, NH3, HCl) have dipoles that do not cancel — the molecule is polar. Use vector addition analogy: arrows in opposite directions cancel; arrows in the same direction add up.

elaborate.description: Students determine molecular polarity for 6 molecules: BF3, CHCl3, SO2, CH4, PH3, and HF. For each, they draw the Lewis structure, determine geometry, draw dipole arrows, and conclude polar or nonpolar. Students discuss why CHCl3 is polar while CCl4 is not, even though both contain polar C-Cl bonds.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Is a C-O bond polar or nonpolar? Justify using electronegativity values. (2) CO2 has two polar bonds but is a nonpolar molecule. Explain. (3) Predict whether SCl2 is polar or nonpolar. Draw the Lewis structure, show molecular geometry, and use dipole arrows to justify.

differentiation.approaching: Provide an electronegativity difference table pre-calculated for common atom pairs; include a visual polarity decision tree: 'Step 1: Are any bonds polar? Step 2: Does the geometry cause them to cancel?'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the bond classification and molecular polarity analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how molecular polarity affects the solubility of vitamins (fat-soluble vs. water-soluble) and explain why vitamin C dissolves in water but vitamin E does not.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual guide showing dipole arrows as colored vectors on 3D molecule drawings; use the tug-of-war analogy with labeled diagrams throughout.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice molecules from 6 to 4; provide pre-drawn Lewis structures and geometries so students focus only on polarity determination; allow use of reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connection to water purification technology: Understanding molecular polarity explains why 'like dissolves like' — polar water dissolves polar/ionic contaminants but not nonpolar oils. Discuss how communities use this principle in oil spill cleanup (using nonpolar absorbents) and water filtration (activated carbon attracts nonpolar pollutants). Highlight environmental justice issues in communities near petrochemical plants.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'polar molecule': Water is a polar molecule because___. CO2 has polar bonds, but the molecule is nonpolar because___. HCl is a polar molecule, so it will dissolve in___.

vocabulary.definition: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally due to a difference in electronegativity between the two atoms
A covalent bond in which electrons are shared equally because the atoms have the same or very similar electronegativity
A separation of positive and negative charge in a molecule, represented by an arrow pointing from the positive end to the negative end
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge due to polar bonds that do not cancel out, resulting in a net dipole
A molecule with an even distribution of charge, either because it has no polar bonds or because the polar bonds cancel due to symmetry
The numerical difference in electronegativity values between two bonded atoms, used to classify bonds as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic

Section 2: Drawing Dipole Arrows on Bonds
Section 3: From Bond Polarity to Molecular Polarity — The Role of Geometry
Section 4: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Molecules — When Dipoles Cancel

cer.phenomenon: When a charged rod is brought near a stream of water, the water bends toward the rod. When the same charged rod is brought near a stream of cooking oil (a mixture of nonpolar molecules), the stream does not bend.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that water bends toward the charged rod because water is a___ molecule, while cooking oil does not bend because it is composed of___ molecules.
cer.evidence_source: Draw the Lewis structure and molecular geometry of water, show the dipole arrows, and explain why the dipoles do not cancel. Compare to a nonpolar molecule like a long hydrocarbon chain.
cer.reasoning_frame: Water has a___ geometry with___ lone pairs, causing the dipole arrows to___. This creates a net___ that is attracted to the charged rod. Cooking oil molecules are___ because___, so they are not attracted to the charged rod.

lessons.title: Intermolecular Forces
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify the types of intermolecular forces present in a substance and rank them by strength to predict physical properties like boiling point.
lessons.circle_prompt: What holds your friend group together? Is it one strong connection or many small ones? Can weak connections add up to be strong?
lessons.do_now: Water boils at 100 degrees C, but methane (CH4) boils at -161 degrees C. Both are small molecules. What is different about how their molecules interact with each other?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter
PS2.B: Types of Interactions

materials: IMF card sorting set (20 molecules with properties, 1 per group)
Boiling point data table for various substances (printed)
Demonstration materials: water, rubbing alcohol, cooking oil in petri dishes for evaporation race

engage.description: Evaporation race demo: Place a drop of water, rubbing alcohol, and acetone on three separate glass slides. Students observe which evaporates fastest. Ask: If evaporation means molecules are escaping from the liquid, which substance has the weakest attraction between its molecules? How can we predict this from molecular structure?

explore.description: Data analysis: Students examine a table showing the boiling points and molecular structures of 12 substances organized into groups: (1) noble gases (He, Ne, Ar — showing increasing BP with size), (2) similar-sized molecules with different polarity (CH4 vs. NH3 vs. H2O), (3) molecules with and without -OH groups. Students look for patterns and formulate hypotheses about what molecular features lead to higher boiling points.

explain.description: Teacher introduces three types of intermolecular forces (IMFs) in order of increasing strength: (1) London dispersion forces (LDFs) — present in ALL molecules, increase with molecular size/electron count; the only IMF in nonpolar substances. (2) Dipole-dipole forces — present in polar molecules; stronger than LDFs for similar-sized molecules. (3) Hydrogen bonding — a strong dipole-dipole force occurring when H is bonded to N, O, or F; explains water's unusually high boiling point. Key distinction: IMFs act BETWEEN molecules; intramolecular bonds (ionic, covalent) act WITHIN molecules.

elaborate.description: IMF card sort: Each group receives 10 molecule cards. For each, students determine: (1) Is it polar or nonpolar? (2) What IMFs are present? (3) Rank the 10 molecules from lowest to highest expected boiling point based on IMF strength. Groups then compare their rankings to actual boiling point data and discuss any surprises.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Identify all intermolecular forces present in HF. (2) Explain why H2O (MW=18) has a much higher boiling point than CH4 (MW=16) even though they are similar in size. (3) Rank these substances from lowest to highest boiling point: Ar, HCl, HF, CH4. Justify.

differentiation.approaching: Provide an IMF identification flowchart: 'Is the molecule polar? If yes, does it have H bonded to N, O, or F? If yes = hydrogen bonding. If no = dipole-dipole. If nonpolar = London dispersion only.' Include a strength ranking reference card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the data analysis and card sorting activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research why ice floats (hydrogen bonding creates an open crystalline structure less dense than liquid water) and explain the ecological significance of this anomaly for aquatic life.
differentiation.ell: Provide the IMF flowchart with visual diagrams showing each type of IMF at the molecular level; include bilingual labels on all card sorting materials.
differentiation.iep: Reduce card sort from 10 molecules to 6; provide a pre-completed example for each type of IMF; allow use of flowchart and reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connection to gecko adhesion: Geckos can climb smooth glass walls using London dispersion forces between billions of tiny hairs (setae) on their feet and the surface. Engineers are developing gecko-inspired adhesives — connecting molecular forces to biomimicry in engineering. Discuss how indigenous observations of nature have long inspired innovation.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'intermolecular forces': Water has an unusually high boiling point for its size because___. Both CH4 and H2O are small molecules, but water boils at 100 degrees C while methane boils at -161 degrees C because___. London dispersion forces are the weakest type of IMF, so substances that only have LDFs tend to___.

vocabulary.definition: The relatively weak forces of attraction between molecules (as opposed to intramolecular bonds within molecules)
Weak, temporary attractive forces between all molecules caused by momentary uneven electron distributions; strength increases with molecular size
Attractive forces between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another polar molecule
A strong type of dipole-dipole attraction that occurs when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine and is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F
The temperature at which the vapor pressure of a liquid equals atmospheric pressure; higher IMF strength leads to higher boiling points
A strong bond within a molecule (ionic, covalent, or metallic) as opposed to weaker intermolecular forces between molecules

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Intermolecular vs. Intramolecular Forces — What's the Difference?
Section 2: London Dispersion Forces — Present in Everything
Section 3: Dipole-Dipole Forces — Polar Molecules Attract
Section 4: Hydrogen Bonding — The Strongest IMF
Section 5: Predicting Physical Properties from IMF Strength

cer.phenomenon: Ethanol (C2H5OH, MW=46) has a boiling point of 78 degrees C, while dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3, MW=46) has a boiling point of -24 degrees C. Both molecules have the same molecular formula (C2H6O) and the same molecular weight, but vastly different boiling points.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that ethanol has a much higher boiling point than dimethyl ether because___.
cer.evidence_source: Examine the structural formulas of both molecules, identify the intermolecular forces present in each, and explain how the presence of the -OH group in ethanol creates an additional type of IMF.
cer.reasoning_frame: Ethanol has an -OH group, which allows it to form___ with neighboring molecules because___. Dimethyl ether lacks an -OH group, so its strongest IMF is___. Since hydrogen bonds are___ than dipole-dipole forces, ethanol requires___ energy to boil, resulting in a___ boiling point.

lessons.title: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can predict the melting point, solubility, and conductivity of a substance based on its type of bonding and intermolecular forces.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about how the smallest details can have the biggest effects. What is something tiny in your life that has a huge impact?
lessons.do_now: Diamond and graphite are both made entirely of carbon atoms. Diamond is the hardest known natural substance, while graphite is soft enough to use as pencil lead. How can the same element have such different properties?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Substance cards with structure diagrams and property data (20 cards)
Sorting mats (ionic, molecular, network covalent, metallic)
Samples if available: NaCl, sugar, paraffin wax, copper wire, graphite pencil
Reference table of common substances and their properties

engage.description: Show four substances: a salt crystal, a sugar cube, a copper wire, and a piece of graphite. State their melting points: NaCl = 801 degrees C, sugar = 186 degrees C, copper = 1085 degrees C, graphite > 3600 degrees C. Ask: Can you predict which type of bonding each has just from the melting point? What patterns do you see?

explore.description: Substance sorting challenge: Each group receives 12 substance cards, each showing the substance name, a particle-level structure diagram, melting point, conductivity data, and solubility in water. Students sort the cards into four categories (ionic, molecular, network covalent, metallic) using the property data as evidence. They must justify each placement.

explain.description: Teacher builds a comprehensive property summary: (1) Ionic — high MP, soluble in water, conducts when dissolved/melted. (2) Molecular — low MP, may or may not dissolve in water (polar dissolves in water, nonpolar does not), does not conduct. (3) Network covalent — very high MP, insoluble, does not conduct (except graphite). (4) Metallic — variable MP, insoluble in water, conducts as solid. Key principle: the strength of the forces holding particles together determines the energy needed to overcome them.

elaborate.description: Prediction challenge: Students receive descriptions of 4 unknown substances with partial property data and must predict the missing properties. Example: 'Substance X melts at 2072 degrees C and does not conduct electricity. Predict its solubility in water and what type of bonding it has.' Students write CER-style justifications for each prediction.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) A substance melts at 45 degrees C, does not conduct electricity, and does not dissolve in water. What type of bonding does it most likely have? Explain. (2) Why do network covalent substances like diamond have extremely high melting points? (3) Explain at the particulate level why the smartphone glass in the Regents sample cluster is an insulator.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a property prediction reference card organized by bond type with key properties listed; include guided questions for each sorting card ('Does it conduct? If yes as a solid = metallic. If yes only when dissolved = ionic.').
differentiation.on_level: Complete the substance sorting and prediction challenge as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain the properties of graphene — a single layer of graphite — and why it conducts electricity (delocalized pi electrons) while diamond does not, despite both being pure carbon.
differentiation.ell: Provide sorting mats with property checklists in bilingual format; include particle-level diagrams on each sorting mat showing the bond type visually.
differentiation.iep: Reduce sorting cards from 12 to 8; provide a completed example card in each category; allow use of all reference materials during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to the smartphone chemistry cluster from the Regents exam: aluminosilicate glass (network covalent/ionic), indium tin oxide conductor (metallic), lithium battery (ionic/metallic). Discuss how understanding structure-property relationships enables material scientists — many of whom come from underrepresented backgrounds like Mildred Dresselhaus, the 'Queen of Carbon Science' — to design new materials for technology.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'structure-property relationship': Diamond has an extremely high melting point because___. Both diamond and table salt have crystal lattice structures, but they melt at very different temperatures because___. The particulate-level structure of a substance determines its bulk properties, so knowing the bonding type allows us to___.

vocabulary.definition: A substance in which atoms are connected by covalent bonds in a continuous three-dimensional network, resulting in very high melting points and hardness
A substance composed of discrete molecules held together by intermolecular forces, resulting in relatively low melting points
Observable, macroscopic properties of a substance (melting point, conductivity, solubility) that result from its particulate-level structure
The atomic or molecular scale at which bonding and intermolecular forces operate
A substance that allows the flow of electrical current, due to the presence of mobile charged particles (free electrons or ions)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Four Categories of Solids — Ionic, Molecular, Network Covalent, Metallic
Section 2: Predicting Melting Point from Bonding Type and IMF Strength
Section 3: Conductivity — When and Why Substances Conduct
Section 4: Solubility — Like Dissolves Like
Section 5: From Particulate Structure to Bulk Properties — The Big Picture

cer.phenomenon: The screen of a smartphone is made of aluminosilicate glass, a network of silicon, oxygen, and aluminum atoms bonded covalently. The screen is coated with a thin layer of indium tin oxide (ITO), which is a metallic conductor. The glass is an insulator, but the ITO coating makes it a responsive touch screen.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the aluminosilicate glass is an insulator because___, while the ITO coating conducts electricity because___.
cer.evidence_source: Describe the bonding and structure of each material and explain how the type of bonding determines whether mobile charged particles are available for electrical conduction.
cer.reasoning_frame: In aluminosilicate glass, the atoms are bonded in a___ network where electrons are___, so there are no mobile charges to carry current. In ITO, the___ bonding means electrons are___, allowing them to flow when voltage is applied. This explains why the glass provides___ while the ITO provides___.

lessons.title: Bonding and Structure Unit Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can analyze an unknown substance's properties and systematically determine its bond type, molecular geometry, polarity, and intermolecular forces.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could explain one chemistry concept to someone who has never taken the class, which topic from this unit would you choose and why?
lessons.do_now: Quick review challenge: Classify each substance as ionic, metallic, molecular, or network covalent based on one clue. (a) Melts at 3500 degrees C, does not conduct. (b) Shiny, malleable, conducts. (c) Melts at 80 degrees C, dissolves in water. (d) Dissolves in water, conducts when dissolved, MP = 1074 degrees C.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter
PS2.B: Types of Interactions

materials: Substance mystery challenge cards (4 sets for group rotation)
Reference table and periodic table (1 each per student)

engage.description: Present the 'Bonding Detective' challenge: A forensic scientist receives four unknown white powders from a crime scene. Using only property tests (melting point, conductivity, solubility, crystal structure), they must determine what each substance is. Today students will use the same logic to review all bonding concepts.

explore.description: Station rotation review (4 stations, 3 min each): Station 1 — Lewis structure and geometry prediction for 3 molecules. Station 2 — Bond type classification (ionic, polar covalent, nonpolar covalent) for 6 atom pairs using electronegativity. Station 3 — IMF identification and boiling point ranking for 4 substances. Station 4 — Property-to-bonding deduction for 3 unknown substances.

explain.description: Class review and discussion of commonly confused concepts: (1) Bond polarity vs. molecular polarity (CO2 has polar bonds but is nonpolar). (2) IMFs vs. intramolecular bonds (boiling breaks IMFs, not covalent bonds). (3) Why ionic compounds have high melting points but molecular compounds do not (lattice of ions vs. weak IMFs between molecules). Address student questions from station work.

elaborate.description: Concept map construction: Students create a concept map connecting all major terms from the unit: ionic bond, covalent bond, metallic bond, Lewis structure, VSEPR, molecular geometry, polarity, LDFs, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, melting point, conductivity, solubility. They must use linking phrases to show relationships (e.g., 'determines' 'is caused by' 'leads to').

evaluate.description: Regents-style practice cluster: Students answer a 5-question cluster similar to the smartphone chemistry sample cluster, combining bonding, polarity, IMFs, and property predictions around a real-world phenomenon (materials in a water bottle: HDPE plastic, glass, stainless steel, and the water inside).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed concept map with key terms placed and some linking phrases filled in; include a unit summary reference sheet organized by topic for use during stations.
differentiation.on_level: Complete station rotation, concept map, and practice cluster as designed.
differentiation.advanced: After completing the practice cluster, students write their own 3-question cluster around a new phenomenon (e.g., why does hand sanitizer evaporate so quickly? Why is stainless steel used for surgical tools?) and include an answer key.
differentiation.ell: Provide concept map terms as pre-cut cards that students arrange and connect with arrows; include bilingual linking phrases; allow verbal explanation of concept map relationships.
differentiation.iep: Reduce stations from 4 to 3 with extended time; provide a completed concept map as a study reference; break the practice cluster into individual questions with reference materials available.

lessons.crse_connection: Revisit the unit's anchoring phenomenon through a global lens: Why do different cultures use different materials for cooking vessels? Clay pots (network covalent silicates), cast iron (metallic), copper (metallic), and ceramic (ionic/covalent network) all have different heat conductivity and reactivity with food. Discuss how traditional knowledge about materials aligns with chemistry concepts.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using concepts from the entire unit. Start with: 'Structure determines properties.' Students expand: 'At the particulate level, the type of bonding between atoms — whether ionic, covalent, or metallic — and the intermolecular forces between molecules determine the bulk properties of a substance, including its melting point, conductivity, and solubility in water.'

vocabulary.definition: A strong bond within a molecule or compound (ionic, covalent, or metallic) that holds atoms together
A weaker force of attraction between separate molecules that determines physical properties like boiling point and solubility
The principle that the particulate-level structure of a substance (bonding, geometry, IMFs) determines its observable bulk properties
An observable event in the natural world that can be explained using scientific principles

Section 2: Review — Molecular Geometry and Polarity
Section 3: Review — Intermolecular Forces and Their Effects
Section 4: The Big Idea — From Atoms to Properties
Section 5: Regents Exam Preparation — Analyzing Phenomena-Based Clusters

cer.phenomenon: A reusable water bottle is made of three materials: the bottle body is polypropylene plastic (a molecular substance made of long carbon chains), the cap seal is silicone rubber (a network of silicon and oxygen atoms), and the metal clip is stainless steel (an alloy of iron, chromium, and nickel). Each material was chosen for specific properties.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the bonding and structure of each material explains why it was chosen for its specific function in the water bottle:___.
cer.evidence_source: For each material, identify the bonding type, predict relevant properties (flexibility, durability, corrosion resistance, weight), and explain why those properties make it suitable for its function.
cer.reasoning_frame: Polypropylene is used for the bottle body because its___ bonding and___ IMFs make it___. Silicone is used for the seal because its___ structure makes it___. Stainless steel is used for the clip because its___ bonding provides___, which is necessary for___.

units.title: Chemical Formulas, Nomenclature & the Mole
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A pharmaceutical company must produce exactly 500 mg tablets of aspirin (C9H8O4). How do chemists count atoms and molecules that are too small to see, and how do they ensure each tablet contains the correct amount?
essential_questions: How do we name and write formulas for chemical compounds?
How can we count particles too small to see using the mole concept?
How do we determine the chemical formula of a compound from experimental data?
units.crse_theme: Students explore the role of precise chemical measurement in industries that affect diverse communities — from pharmaceutical manufacturing in developing nations to water quality testing in underserved communities. The unit highlights the contributions of Amedeo Avogadro and modern analytical chemists from diverse backgrounds.

summative: Unit 4 Exam: Formulas, Nomenclature & the Mole

investigations: Investigation 6: Determining the Empirical Formula of a Hydrate

lessons.title: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write correct chemical formulas for ionic compounds, including those with polyatomic ions, by balancing the charges of cations and anions.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a partnership where both sides have to balance — like a seesaw. What makes a good balance?
lessons.do_now: Sodium forms Na+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. The compound they make is NaCl. Calcium forms Ca2+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. Why is the formula CaCl2 and not CaCl? What rule determines the subscripts?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Ion charge reference card (common cations and anions with charges)
Ion charge cards for criss-cross method practice (laminated, 1 set per group)

engage.description: Show labels from common household products: baking soda (NaHCO3), table salt (NaCl), chalk (CaCO3), plaster of Paris (CaSO4). Ask: What do all these formulas have in common? (They all contain a metal or positive ion paired with a negative ion.) How do chemists know the correct subscripts? Today we learn the formula-writing system.

explore.description: Students practice the criss-cross method for binary ionic compounds: write the cation first, anion second, criss-cross the charges to get subscripts, reduce to lowest ratio. Practice set 1 (binary): NaCl, MgO, Al2O3, CaBr2, K2S, FeCl3. Teacher circulates and provides feedback. Then introduce polyatomic ions: students receive the polyatomic ion reference table and practice formulas with SO4(2-), NO3(-), CO3(2-), OH(-), PO4(3-), NH4(+).

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the rules: (1) Ionic compounds are always neutral — total positive charge equals total negative charge. (2) Use the criss-cross method, then reduce. (3) Polyatomic ions are treated as a single unit — use parentheses when the subscript is greater than 1 (e.g., Ca(OH)2, not CaOH2). (4) Transition metals require Roman numerals in the name to indicate charge (e.g., FeCl2 = iron(II) chloride, FeCl3 = iron(III) chloride).

elaborate.description: Practice set 2 (mixed): Students write formulas for 10 compounds including polyatomic ions and transition metals: ammonium sulfate, calcium phosphate, iron(III) oxide, copper(II) nitrate, aluminum hydroxide. Then reverse: given the formula Mg3(PO4)2, students identify the ions and their charges.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the formula for aluminum sulfate. (2) Write the formula for iron(II) hydroxide. (3) What is wrong with the formula NaCl2? Explain why this formula is incorrect for a compound of sodium and chlorine.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step criss-cross method template with numbered boxes; include a common ion charge chart color-coded by charge; work through the first two problems of each set as a class.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the formula writing practice as designed with the ion reference card.
differentiation.advanced: Write formulas for compounds with transition metals that have multiple oxidation states without being given the charge (e.g., determine the charge of iron in Fe2O3 from the formula).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual criss-cross method guide with arrows and color-coded charges; allow verbal explanation of the error in NaCl2; bilingual ion reference card.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice sets from 6+10 to 4+6; provide a pre-organized workspace with columns for cation, anion, charges, and final formula; allow use of reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how chemical formulas are a universal language — a chemist in Japan, Nigeria, and Brazil all read NaCl the same way. Connect to the development of chemical notation by Jons Jacob Berzelius (Sweden, 1813), who replaced alchemical symbols with the letter-based system we still use today. Discuss how alchemical traditions existed in many cultures: Chinese alchemy, Islamic alchemy (jabir ibn Hayyan), and European alchemy.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'chemical formula': The formula for calcium chloride is CaCl2 because___. Both sodium and calcium form ionic compounds with chlorine, but their formulas are different because___. An ionic compound must be electrically neutral, so the formula for aluminum oxide is___.

vocabulary.definition: A representation of a compound using element symbols and subscripts to show the ratio of atoms
A number written below and to the right of an element symbol in a formula, indicating the number of atoms of that element
A charged group of two or more atoms covalently bonded together that acts as a single ion
A technique for writing ionic compound formulas by crossing the numerical charges of the ions to become subscripts
A compound composed of only two different elements
The charge an atom would have if all bonds were completely ionic; for transition metals, indicated by Roman numerals

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Ionic Compound Formulas — Balancing Charges
Section 2: The Criss-Cross Method for Binary Ionic Compounds
Section 3: Polyatomic Ions — Formulas with Parentheses
Section 4: Transition Metals and Roman Numeral Notation
Section 5: Practice — Writing Formulas from Ion Names

cer.phenomenon: A student writes the formula for magnesium nitrate as MgNO3. Their lab partner says it should be Mg(NO3)2. Both students agree that magnesium forms Mg2+ ions and nitrate is NO3-.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the correct formula is___ because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the charges of Mg2+ and NO3- to demonstrate why two nitrate ions are needed per magnesium ion, and explain when parentheses are required.
cer.reasoning_frame: The ionic compound must be electrically neutral. Mg2+ has a charge of___, and NO3- has a charge of___. To balance, we need___ nitrate ions for every___ magnesium ion. Parentheses are needed because___, giving the correct formula___.

lessons.title: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can name ionic compounds (including those with polyatomic ions and transition metals) and covalent compounds using IUPAC nomenclature rules.
lessons.circle_prompt: Naming things gives them identity. What is the story behind your name — who named you and why?
lessons.do_now: Match these common names to their chemical names: (a) table salt, (b) baking soda, (c) water, (d) rust. Choices: sodium chloride, iron(III) oxide, dihydrogen monoxide, sodium hydrogen carbonate. What patterns do you notice in the chemical names?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Greek prefix chart for covalent naming (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-)

engage.description: Show two chemical labels side by side: 'dihydrogen monoxide' and 'H2O.' Ask: Would you drink something called dihydrogen monoxide? (Students often say no, thinking it sounds dangerous.) Reveal it is water. Discuss why systematic naming matters — it tells us exactly what is in a compound, but common names can be misleading.

explore.description: Two-part naming practice. Part A — Ionic compounds: Students name 8 ionic compounds from formulas using the rules: metal name + nonmetal name with '-ide' ending (NaCl = sodium chloride); polyatomic ions keep their names (CaCO3 = calcium carbonate); transition metals get Roman numerals (FeCl3 = iron(III) chloride). Part B — Covalent compounds: Students name 6 covalent compounds using Greek prefixes (CO2 = carbon dioxide; N2O4 = dinitrogen tetroxide; PCl5 = phosphorus pentachloride).

explain.description: Teacher summarizes the two naming systems. Key distinction: Ionic compounds never use Greek prefixes (not 'disodium monoxide' — just 'sodium oxide'). Covalent compounds use Greek prefixes because two nonmetals can form multiple compounds (CO vs. CO2). Review common mistakes: forgetting Roman numerals for transition metals, using prefixes for ionic compounds, not changing the second element's ending to '-ide' for binary compounds.

elaborate.description: Nomenclature card matching game: In pairs, students match 20 compound name cards with their formula cards. Cards include a mix of ionic (binary and polyatomic) and covalent compounds. After matching, they sort the pairs into 'ionic' and 'covalent' categories and identify the clues that distinguish them.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Name these compounds: CuSO4, PCl3, Al2O3, N2O5. (2) Write the formula for: potassium permanganate, dinitrogen trioxide, calcium hydroxide. (3) A student names MgCl2 as 'magnesium dichloride.' What is wrong, and what is the correct name?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a naming decision tree: 'Is there a metal? If yes = ionic naming. If no = covalent naming with prefixes.' Include a worked example for each naming type at the top of the worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete both naming practice sections and the card matching game as designed.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the IUPAC naming system was established as an international standard by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which includes scientists from over 50 countries. Before IUPAC, the same compound could have different names in different countries, leading to confusion. Connect to the importance of standardized communication in global science.

Students write appositive sentences for three additional compounds: sodium hydroxide (lye/drain cleaner), silicon dioxide (sand/quartz), and dihydrogen monoxide (water).

A compound composed of exactly two different elements
Number prefixes (mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa) used to name covalent compounds to indicate the number of each atom

lessons.title: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain what a mole is, use Avogadro's number to convert between moles and particles, and explain why chemists need the mole as a counting unit.
lessons.circle_prompt: We use words like 'dozen' (12) and 'pair' (2) to count everyday objects. What would you need a really, really large counting word for?
lessons.do_now: A single grain of sand has a mass of about 0.004 grams. How many grains would you need to equal 1 gram? Now consider: a single carbon atom has a mass of 0.00000000000000000000002 grams. How could a chemist count atoms? There must be a better way.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Mole scale analogy cards (printed — showing relative sizes)
Mole Day celebration props (optional: for October 23, 6:02 AM)

engage.description: Scale challenge: If you had a mole (6.02 x 10^23) of pennies and stacked them, the stack would reach from Earth to the Sun and back over 400 billion times. If you had a mole of grains of sand, it would cover the entire United States to a depth of about 3 feet. Ask: Why would scientists need a number this incredibly large? Because atoms are incredibly small.

explore.description: Students practice mole-to-particle and particle-to-mole conversions using Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23). Practice set: (1) How many molecules are in 2.5 moles of water? (2) How many moles is 3.01 x 10^23 atoms of iron? (3) How many atoms are in 0.75 moles of gold? Students use dimensional analysis setup: given quantity x conversion factor = desired quantity.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: A mole is 6.02 x 10^23 of anything — the chemist's counting unit. Just as a dozen = 12, a mole = 6.02 x 10^23. One mole of any element contains Avogadro's number of atoms. One mole of any molecular compound contains Avogadro's number of molecules. Key: distinguish between atoms and molecules (1 mole of H2O = 6.02 x 10^23 molecules, but 3 x 6.02 x 10^23 atoms because each molecule has 3 atoms).

elaborate.description: Multi-step conversion challenge: (1) How many oxygen atoms are in 2.0 moles of CO2? (Students must first convert moles of CO2 to molecules, then multiply by 2 for the two oxygen atoms per molecule.) (2) If a sample contains 1.806 x 10^24 atoms of hydrogen and all the hydrogen is in the form of H2 gas, how many moles of H2 are present?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Define 'mole' in your own words. (2) How many molecules are in 4.00 moles of CO2? (3) A sample contains 1.204 x 10^24 molecules of water. How many moles is this? How many individual hydrogen atoms does this sample contain?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a dimensional analysis template with blanks: '___ x (6.02 x 10^23 / 1 mol) = ___' and guide students through the first two problems step by step; include a calculator use guide for scientific notation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mole conversion practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate how long it would take to count a mole of objects at a rate of 1 per second, and express the answer in years. Discuss why this illustrates the necessity of the mole concept.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual dimensional analysis setup with arrows showing the conversion path; use the dozen-to-mole analogy with visual comparisons; bilingual vocabulary definitions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems by half; provide a conversion factor reference card; allow calculator use throughout; break multi-step problems into numbered steps.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Amedeo Avogadro (Italian physicist, 1776-1856) whose hypothesis about equal volumes of gases was not accepted during his lifetime but became foundational to chemistry. The number was named in his honor by Jean Baptiste Perrin (French physicist). Discuss how scientific contributions are sometimes recognized only after a scientist's death, and how naming conventions in science honor diverse contributors.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'mole': A mole of any substance contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles because___. A mole of carbon and a mole of gold contain the same number of atoms, but they have different masses because___. Atoms are too small to count individually, so chemists use the mole to___.

vocabulary.definition: The SI unit for amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02 x 10^23 representative particles (atoms, molecules, or formula units)
6.02 x 10^23 — the number of representative particles in one mole of a substance
The smallest unit of a substance: atoms for elements, molecules for covalent compounds, or formula units for ionic compounds
A problem-solving method that uses conversion factors to change from one unit to another while keeping track of units

cer.reasoning_frame: Container A: 12.0 g C / ___ g/mol = ___ mol C x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ atoms. Container B: 55.8 g Fe / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Fe x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ atoms. Both containers hold approximately 1 mole, which contains___ atoms, demonstrating that the mole concept connects___ to___.

lessons.title: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the molar mass of a compound from its formula and convert between moles, mass, and number of particles using dimensional analysis.
lessons.circle_prompt: When you go grocery shopping, some things are sold by weight and others by count (eggs by the dozen, bananas by the bunch). Why do we use different units for different things?
lessons.do_now: The periodic table says carbon has an atomic mass of 12.01 amu and oxygen has 16.00 amu. If CO2 has one carbon and two oxygens, predict the mass of one mole of CO2 molecules. Show your calculation.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Triple-beam balances and element samples for verification (optional)

engage.description: Show students three piles: 12.0 g of carbon (charcoal), 55.8 g of iron filings, and 18.0 g of water. State: Each pile contains the same number of particles — one mole, or 6.02 x 10^23. Ask: Why do they have different masses? Because each atom or molecule has a different mass. The mass of one mole is called the molar mass, and it equals the atomic or formula mass in grams.

explore.description: Students calculate molar masses for 8 compounds: H2O, NaCl, CO2, C6H12O6 (glucose), Ca(OH)2, Fe2O3, H2SO4, and C9H8O4 (aspirin — connecting to the anchoring phenomenon). They show all work: list each element, multiply atomic mass by number of atoms, sum all contributions.

explain.description: Teacher presents the mole conversion 'road map': Particles <-> (Avogadro's number) <-> Moles <-> (Molar mass) <-> Grams. All conversions use dimensional analysis. Work through three example problems: (1) How many grams are in 3.50 moles of NaCl? (2) How many moles are in 25.0 g of water? (3) How many molecules are in 10.0 g of CO2? (This requires two steps: grams to moles, then moles to molecules.)

elaborate.description: Aspirin tablet challenge (connecting to the anchoring phenomenon): A 500 mg aspirin tablet contains 500 mg of C9H8O4. Students calculate: (1) the molar mass of aspirin, (2) how many moles of aspirin are in one tablet, (3) how many molecules of aspirin are in one tablet, (4) how many individual atoms of all types are in one tablet.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the molar mass of calcium phosphate, Ca3(PO4)2. (2) How many grams are in 0.250 moles of glucose (C6H12O6)? (3) A sample has a mass of 44.0 g of CO2. How many moles is this, and how many oxygen atoms does it contain?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a molar mass calculation template with columns: element, atomic mass, number of atoms, subtotal; include the road map diagram with arrows and conversion factor labels for reference.
differentiation.on_level: Complete molar mass calculations and conversion problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Determine how many aspirin tablets a pharmaceutical company can produce from 1.00 kg of pure aspirin, and calculate the total number of molecules in the entire batch.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual road map with color-coded conversion arrows and worked examples in each direction; include bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce the number of molar mass calculations from 8 to 5; provide a molar mass example card; break multi-step problems into sequential numbered steps; allow calculator throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to the pharmaceutical industry: Precision in measuring moles and masses is critical in drug manufacturing. Discuss how access to affordable medication varies globally — the same aspirin formula costs different amounts in different countries. Highlight the work of organizations like Doctors Without Borders that rely on precise chemical manufacturing to provide medications to underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'molar mass': The molar mass of water is 18.02 g/mol because___. One mole of carbon and one mole of iron contain the same number of atoms, but their masses are different because___. To convert from grams to moles, you divide by the molar mass, so 44.0 g of CO2 equals___.

vocabulary.definition: The mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol), numerically equal to the formula mass in amu
The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a chemical formula, expressed in atomic mass units (amu)
A ratio of equivalent measurements used to convert from one unit to another in dimensional analysis
A visual tool showing the conversion pathway between particles, moles, and grams using Avogadro's number and molar mass
