cer.phenomenon: A 500 mg aspirin tablet (C9H8O4) seems like a tiny amount of material. Yet it contains approximately 1.67 x 10^21 molecules — far more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth (estimated at 7.5 x 10^18).
cer.claim_starter: I claim that a tiny 500 mg aspirin tablet contains___ molecules, which is more than the number of grains of sand on Earth, because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of aspirin, convert 500 mg to moles, then convert moles to molecules using Avogadro's number. Compare to the estimated number of sand grains.
cer.reasoning_frame: The molar mass of aspirin is___ g/mol. 500 mg = ___ g, which equals___ moles. Multiplying by Avogadro's number: ___ x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ molecules. This is larger than 7.5 x 10^18 sand grains because atoms and molecules are___, so even a small mass contains___.

lessons.title: Percent Composition
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the percent composition of each element in a compound from its chemical formula.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to describe the composition of your ideal pizza by percentage — what percent crust, sauce, cheese, toppings — what would it be?
lessons.do_now: A compound has the formula H2O. It contains hydrogen and oxygen. Without calculating, predict: Is water mostly hydrogen or mostly oxygen by mass? (Hint: Think about the atomic masses.) Write your prediction and reasoning.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

engage.description: Show a nutrition label from a food package. Ask: What does 'percent daily value' mean? It tells you what fraction of your daily needs is in one serving. Chemists use percent composition the same way — to describe what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element. This is used in mining (what percent of ore is useful metal?), nutrition (what percent of a compound is a useful element?), and forensics.

explore.description: Students calculate percent composition for 5 compounds: H2O, NaCl, CO2, C6H12O6, and Fe2O3. Process: (1) Find molar mass of compound. (2) Find total mass contribution of each element (atomic mass x number of atoms). (3) Divide element mass by total molar mass x 100%. Students verify that all percentages add to 100% (within rounding). They create pie charts for two of the compounds.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the percent composition formula: %element = (mass of element in one mole of compound / molar mass of compound) x 100%. Discuss real-world applications: iron ore analysis (what % of Fe2O3 is iron? 69.9% — this tells miners the maximum iron they can extract), and fertilizer labels (N-P-K numbers represent percent nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium by mass).

elaborate.description: Application problems: (1) A mining company has 500 kg of hematite ore (Fe2O3). What is the maximum mass of iron that can be extracted? (2) A fertilizer bag says it is 46% nitrogen by mass and lists the compound as CO(NH2)2 (urea). Verify this percentage. (3) Two iron compounds: FeO and Fe2O3. Which contains a higher percentage of iron?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the percent composition of each element in calcium carbonate (CaCO3). (2) A compound is 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Does this match the percent composition of ethanol (C2H6O)? Show your work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step percent composition template with labeled columns (element, atomic mass, number of atoms, total mass, percent); work through the first example (H2O) as a class.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the percent composition calculations and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given percent composition data for an unknown compound, work backwards to determine a possible molecular formula (preview of empirical formula determination).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual percent composition calculation guide with color-coded steps; use the pizza analogy throughout with labeled diagrams; bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice compounds from 5 to 3; reduce application problems from 3 to 2; provide a molar mass reference for common compounds; allow calculator and periodic table during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how percent composition is critical in mining and resource extraction — connecting to the global demand for lithium (Li2CO3 in batteries) and the environmental and social impact of lithium mining on indigenous communities in Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina (the 'Lithium Triangle'). Chemistry concepts have real consequences for real communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'percent composition': Water is 88.9% oxygen by mass because___. Both FeO and Fe2O3 contain iron and oxygen, but they have different percent compositions because___. Knowing the percent composition of an ore tells miners___, so they can___.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage by mass of each element in a compound, calculated by dividing the mass of each element in one mole by the molar mass of the compound and multiplying by 100%
The ratio of the mass of one component to the total mass of a mixture or compound

lessons.title: Empirical and Molecular Formulas
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can determine the empirical formula of a compound from percent composition data and use molar mass to find the molecular formula.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever simplified a recipe — like doubling or halving it? How do you keep the proportions the same when you scale up or down?
lessons.do_now: Two compounds both contain only carbon and hydrogen. Compound A is 75.0% carbon and 25.0% hydrogen. Compound B is also 75.0% carbon and 25.0% hydrogen, but Compound B's molar mass is twice as large. Can they have the same formula? Discuss with your partner.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Lab data cards (simulated experimental data for 4 unknown compounds)

engage.description: Present a mystery: Formaldehyde (CH2O, molar mass 30), acetic acid (C2H4O2, molar mass 60), and glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180) all have the same percent composition: 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. How is this possible? They all have the same simplest ratio of atoms (1:2:1) but different actual numbers. The simplest ratio is the empirical formula; the actual number is the molecular formula.

explore.description: Step-by-step empirical formula determination: Students practice with two compounds. (1) A compound is 63.5% Fe and 36.5% O. Convert percentages to grams (assume 100 g sample), divide by atomic mass to get moles, divide by smallest mole value to get the ratio, round to nearest whole number. Result: Fe2O3. (2) A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Result: CH2O.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the process: (1) Assume 100 g sample (so percentages become grams). (2) Convert grams to moles for each element. (3) Divide each by the smallest number of moles. (4) If ratios are not whole numbers, multiply all by the smallest integer that gives whole numbers (e.g., 1.5 -> multiply all by 2). For molecular formula: (5) Divide the given molar mass by the empirical formula mass to get the multiplier. (6) Multiply all subscripts by the multiplier.

elaborate.description: Lab data card challenge: Students receive simulated lab data for 4 unknown compounds (percent composition from combustion analysis or decomposition experiments). They determine the empirical formula for each. For 2 of the 4, they are also given the molar mass and must find the molecular formula. One example connects to the anchoring phenomenon: determine the molecular formula of aspirin from percent composition data and molar mass 180.16.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) A compound is 82.8% carbon and 17.2% hydrogen. Determine the empirical formula. (2) If the molar mass of the compound in question 1 is 58.12 g/mol, what is the molecular formula? (3) Explain in one sentence the difference between an empirical formula and a molecular formula.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded step-by-step template with boxes for each calculation step; include a 'common ratios to watch for' card (1.33 -> multiply by 3, 1.5 -> multiply by 2, 1.25 -> multiply by 4).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the empirical formula practice and lab data card challenge as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given combustion analysis data (mass of CO2 and H2O produced from burning a sample), determine the empirical formula of an unknown hydrocarbon.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual flowchart showing the empirical formula process with arrows and color-coded steps; include bilingual calculation templates.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 empirical formula problems plus 1 molecular formula; provide a completed example showing every step; allow use of all reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how empirical formula determination was historically critical in identifying new substances — Justus von Liebig and Friedrich Wohler (Germany, 1800s) developed combustion analysis to determine the composition of organic compounds. This technique was later refined by scientists worldwide and remains essential in pharmaceutical development, helping identify new drug compounds from natural sources used in traditional medicine across cultures.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'empirical formula': CH2O is the empirical formula for glucose, formaldehyde, and acetic acid because___. These three compounds have the same empirical formula, but they are different substances because___. The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so if the empirical formula mass is 30 and the molar mass is 180, the multiplier is___.

vocabulary.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound
An experimental technique that determines the percent composition of a compound by burning it and measuring the products
The ratio of moles of one substance to moles of another, used in formula determination and stoichiometry

lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever seen something dramatic happen — like a firework, a cooking mishap, or rust appearing on metal? What made you think something chemical was going on?
lessons.do_now: Two clear, colorless solutions are mixed together and a bright yellow solid forms at the bottom of the beaker. List all the evidence that a chemical reaction occurred. Predict: Will the mass of the products equal the mass of the reactants? Why or why not?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions (teacher demo only)

engage.description: Teacher demo: Mix lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions in a beaker — an instant bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide forms (the 'golden rain' demo). Students identify all evidence of a chemical reaction (color change, precipitate formation). Then ask: Did matter appear from nothing? Where did the yellow solid come from?

explore.description: Conservation of mass lab: Students measure the mass of a sealed bag containing baking soda and a small cup of vinegar. They tilt the bag to mix the reactants (gas produced, bag inflates). They measure the mass again. Students record before and after masses. Then teacher demo: burn steel wool on a balance — mass increases slightly. Discuss: Where did the extra mass come from? (Oxygen from air bonded to iron.)

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789): In a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed — the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. At the atomic level, atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. This is why chemical equations must be balanced — same number of each type of atom on both sides.

elaborate.description: Students analyze three scenarios where it appears mass is not conserved and explain why it actually is: (1) Burning wood produces ash that weighs less than the wood (gases escaped — CO2 and H2O). (2) A nail rusts and becomes heavier (gained oxygen from air). (3) Baking soda + vinegar in an open container loses mass (CO2 gas escaped). Students explain each using conservation of mass.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) State the Law of Conservation of Mass in your own words. (2) A 10.0 g piece of magnesium is burned in air and produces 16.6 g of magnesium oxide. What mass of oxygen reacted? (3) In the Regents sample cluster about blueberry fields, students are asked to 'cite numerical evidence to demonstrate the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved.' Explain what this means.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a data table template with before/after mass columns and a 'difference' column; include a sentence frame: 'Mass was conserved because___ equals___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the conservation of mass lab and scenario analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design an experiment to prove conservation of mass for a reaction that produces a gas, accounting for how to capture and measure the gas.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual diagram of the baking soda + vinegar reaction with labeled before/after particle models; bilingual sentence frames for the exit ticket.
differentiation.iep: Pair with a lab partner; provide a simplified data table with guiding questions at each step; reduce scenario analysis from 3 to 2.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Antoine Lavoisier, the 'father of modern chemistry,' who established the Law of Conservation of Mass. Also discuss his wife Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, who was his essential collaborator — translating scientific texts, illustrating experiments, and managing the lab — yet received little credit for decades. Connect to the invisible labor of women and marginalized collaborators in science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'conservation of mass': When wood burns, the ash weighs less than the original wood because___. It seems like mass disappears during burning, but mass is actually conserved because___. Atoms are rearranged during a chemical reaction but not created or destroyed, so the total mass of products___.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which one or more substances (reactants) are converted into one or more new substances (products) with different properties
A substance that enters into and is changed by a chemical reaction, written on the left side of a chemical equation
A substance that is formed as a result of a chemical reaction, written on the right side of a chemical equation
In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products; matter is neither created nor destroyed
An insoluble solid that forms when two aqueous solutions are mixed

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Evidence of Chemical Reactions — Five Key Indicators
Section 2: The Law of Conservation of Mass
Section 3: Atoms Are Rearranged, Not Created or Destroyed
Section 4: Apparent Violations of Conservation — Explaining the Exceptions

cer.phenomenon: A student places an open beaker containing baking soda on a balance and records a mass of 85.0 g. They add vinegar and observe bubbling. After the reaction stops, the balance reads 82.3 g. The student concludes that mass was not conserved.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's conclusion is incorrect because mass was conserved, but___ explains the apparent loss of 2.7 g.
cer.evidence_source: Identify the gas produced in the reaction (CO2), explain why it escaped the open beaker, and describe how the experiment could be redesigned to demonstrate conservation of mass.
cer.reasoning_frame: The reaction between baking soda and vinegar produces___ gas, which is___ and escaped the open beaker into the air. The 'missing' 2.7 g is the mass of the___. If the reaction were conducted in a___, the mass before and after would be___, demonstrating that___.

lessons.title: Balancing Chemical Equations
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can balance chemical equations by adjusting coefficients to ensure the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you had to make things 'come out even' — dividing food equally, splitting a bill, balancing a budget. What strategies did you use?
lessons.do_now: The unbalanced equation is: _Fe + _O2 -> _Fe2O3. Count the atoms on each side. What is unbalanced? Try adding numbers in front of the formulas (not changing subscripts) to make both sides equal.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Atom counting chips or colored tiles (for visual balancing)

engage.description: Visual demo: Show the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O using molecular model kits. Build 1 H2 and 1 O2 on the left, and try to build H2O on the right. Problem: you have 2 oxygen atoms but only need 1 for H2O. You cannot break the O2 (that would change the formula). Solution: make 2 H2O molecules, but now you need 2 H2 molecules. Final: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Students see the physical reason for coefficients.

explore.description: Level 1 balancing practice: Students balance 8 equations starting simple (synthesis and decomposition) and progressing to moderate difficulty. Strategy guide: (1) Start with the most complex formula. (2) Balance metals first, then nonmetals, then oxygen, then hydrogen. (3) Never change subscripts — only add coefficients. (4) Check your work by counting all atoms on both sides. Students use whiteboards for quick practice and teacher circulation.

explain.description: Teacher reviews common balancing strategies and addresses errors: changing subscripts vs. coefficients (subscripts change the compound, coefficients change the amount), dealing with polyatomic ions that appear intact on both sides (balance them as a unit), and handling odd-even mismatches (e.g., if you have an odd oxygen on one side and O2 on the other, double everything first).

elaborate.description: Level 2 balancing practice: 6 more challenging equations including combustion reactions (hydrocarbons + O2 -> CO2 + H2O), reactions with polyatomic ions, and equations requiring larger coefficients. Students work in pairs and compare strategies.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Balance these three equations and prove they are balanced by counting all atoms: (1) _Al + _HCl -> _AlCl3 + _H2 (2) _C3H8 + _O2 -> _CO2 + _H2O (3) _Ca(OH)2 + _H3PO4 -> _Ca3(PO4)2 + _H2O

differentiation.approaching: Provide atom counting chips (colored tiles representing different elements) so students can physically manipulate the atoms; include a pre-made atom counting table for each equation with rows for each element.
differentiation.on_level: Complete Level 1 and Level 2 balancing practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Balance oxidation-reduction (redox) equations using the half-reaction method (preview of electrochemistry).
differentiation.ell: Provide visual balancing guides with color-coded atoms and arrows showing where coefficients go; include bilingual strategy cards.
differentiation.iep: Reduce Level 1 to 5 equations and Level 2 to 3 equations; provide an atom counting template for each equation; allow use of strategy card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect equation balancing to the Regents sample cluster on blueberry fields, where students must 'cite numerical evidence from Equation 3 to demonstrate the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved.' Emphasize that this skill is tested directly on the new Regents exam in a phenomena-driven context.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'balanced equation': We use coefficients instead of changing subscripts because___. The unbalanced equation H2 + O2 -> H2O has 2 oxygen atoms on the left but only 1 on the right, so___. A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides because___.

vocabulary.definition: A symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulas and symbols to show reactants, products, and their physical states
A number placed in front of a chemical formula in a balanced equation that indicates the number of molecules or formula units of that substance
A chemical equation in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides, satisfying the Law of Conservation of Mass
A number in a chemical formula that indicates the number of atoms of the preceding element; cannot be changed when balancing
The arrow in a chemical equation pointing from reactants to products, read as 'produces' or 'yields'

Section 2: Coefficients vs. Subscripts — What You Can and Cannot Change
Section 3: Step-by-Step Balancing Strategy
Section 4: Balancing Combustion Reactions and Polyatomic Ion Equations
Section 5: Checking Your Work — Atom Counting

cer.phenomenon: A student is given the unbalanced equation for the combustion of propane in a gas grill: C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. They write the balanced equation as C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O. Their lab partner says the oxygen is wrong.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the correctly balanced equation is___ because counting atoms on both sides shows___.
cer.evidence_source: Count every atom on both sides of the student's proposed equation, identify the error, and determine the correct coefficients.
cer.reasoning_frame: In the student's equation, the left side has C=___, H=___, O=___. The right side has C=___, H=___, O=___. The___ are not balanced because___. The correct equation is___, which has___ atoms of each element on both sides.

lessons.title: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify chemical reactions as synthesis, decomposition, or combustion and predict products for each type.
lessons.circle_prompt: Building something up, breaking something down, and burning something — which of these three processes do you do most often in daily life?
lessons.do_now: Classify each scenario: (a) Two elements combine to form a compound. (b) A compound breaks apart into simpler substances. (c) A substance burns in oxygen. Write one real-world example for each.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Demo materials: steel wool + O2, hydrogen peroxide + MnO2 catalyst, candle burning

engage.description: Three quick demos: (1) Synthesis — burn steel wool in oxygen (2Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3 sparks). (2) Decomposition — add MnO2 to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2 -> H2O + O2, rapid bubbling). (3) Combustion — light a candle (wax + O2 -> CO2 + H2O). Ask: What pattern do you see in each type? Students turn-and-talk.

explore.description: Students examine 12 balanced equations and classify each as synthesis (A + B -> AB), decomposition (AB -> A + B), or combustion (CxHy + O2 -> CO2 + H2O). They identify the pattern for each type: synthesis combines simpler substances into one, decomposition breaks one compound into simpler substances, combustion always involves a fuel reacting with O2 to produce CO2 and H2O. Students then predict products for 4 unwritten reactions.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the three reaction types with general equations. Synthesis: A + B -> AB (two or more substances combine to form one product). Decomposition: AB -> A + B (one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances). Combustion: hydrocarbon + O2 -> CO2 + H2O (always produces carbon dioxide and water). Key connection to the Regents gas stoves cluster: combustion of methane (CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O) and its environmental impact.

elaborate.description: Application problems: (1) In the airbag phenomenon, sodium azide decomposes: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Classify this reaction and explain why it is useful (produces a large volume of inert gas quickly). (2) Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Is this synthesis or something else? (Discuss how some reactions do not fit neatly into one category.) (3) Predict the products of the combustion of ethanol (C2H5OH).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Classify and balance: Mg + N2 -> Mg3N2. (2) Predict the products and balance: C2H6 + O2 -> ___. (3) The Regents gas stoves cluster states that 'a student incorrectly identifies the products of the combustion of methane as oxygen and water.' Write the correct products and explain the error using patterns of chemical properties.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a reaction type decision tree: 'How many reactants? How many products? Is O2 a reactant with a hydrocarbon?' with examples for each branch.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the classification practice and product prediction as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain how the combustion of different fuels (methane, octane, ethanol) produces different amounts of CO2 per unit of energy, connecting to carbon footprint calculations.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual reaction type chart with diagrams using colored blocks (A + B -> AB for synthesis) and real-world photo examples; bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Reduce classification practice from 12 to 8 equations; provide the reaction type patterns on a reference card; allow use of reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of fireworks — a celebration of synthesis and combustion reactions used across cultures: invented in China over 1,000 years ago, central to Diwali celebrations in South Asia, used in New Year celebrations worldwide, and integral to Fourth of July traditions. Different metal salts produce different colors (Sr = red, Ba = green, Cu = blue) through synthesis reactions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'combustion': The combustion of methane produces CO2 and H2O because___. Both synthesis and combustion require energy to start, but combustion always involves___ as a reactant, so___. The decomposition of sodium azide produces nitrogen gas, so it is used in airbags because___.

vocabulary.definition: A reaction in which two or more simple substances combine to form a single, more complex product (A + B -> AB)
A reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances (AB -> A + B)
A rapid reaction between a substance (usually a hydrocarbon) and oxygen that produces carbon dioxide, water, and energy
An organic compound composed of only carbon and hydrogen atoms

Section 2: Decomposition Reactions — Breaking Down
Section 3: Combustion Reactions — Burning with Oxygen

cer.phenomenon: New York State banned gas stoves powered by methane in new residential construction. Methane (CH4) undergoes combustion when burned in a stove. A student incorrectly predicts that the products of methane combustion are oxygen and water.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the correct products of methane combustion are___ and___, not oxygen and water, because combustion reactions follow the pattern___.
cer.evidence_source: Write the balanced equation for the combustion of methane. Use patterns of chemical properties (combustion always produces CO2 and H2O) to correct the student's error.
cer.reasoning_frame: Combustion reactions always involve a hydrocarbon reacting with___ to produce___ and___. Methane is a hydrocarbon (CH4), so: CH4 + 2O2 ->___. The student's error was predicting___ as a product, but oxygen is actually a___ in combustion, not a product. This matters environmentally because___ is a greenhouse gas.

lessons.title: Single and Double Replacement Reactions
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify reactions as single or double replacement, use the activity series to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur, and use solubility rules to predict precipitates in double replacement reactions.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about switching partners in a dance or trading cards. When does a trade happen, and when does someone refuse? What determines whether a trade is worth it?
lessons.do_now: Prediction: If you place a piece of zinc metal into a solution of copper sulfate (CuSO4, blue solution), what do you think will happen? Will the zinc react? Will anything change color? Draw or describe your prediction.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Activity series reference table (printed and laminated)
Zinc metal strips and copper sulfate solution (for demo or student lab)
Test tubes and solutions for double replacement demo (NaCl + AgNO3)

engage.description: Demo: Place a strip of zinc into copper sulfate solution. Within minutes, students see the zinc become coated with reddish-brown copper and the blue solution begins to fade. Ask: What happened? The zinc 'replaced' the copper in the solution. Zinc is more reactive than copper — it is higher on the activity series. But what if we placed copper into zinc sulfate solution? (Nothing happens — copper is less reactive.)

explore.description: Two-part exploration. Part A — Single replacement: Students use the activity series to predict whether 6 single replacement reactions will occur. For those that do, they write balanced equations. Key rule: a metal will replace a less active metal in solution; a metal will replace hydrogen from an acid if it is above hydrogen on the activity series. Part B — Double replacement: Teacher demos NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl (white precipitate) + NaNO3. Students use solubility rules to identify the precipitate. They practice predicting products and identifying precipitates for 4 additional reactions.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: Single replacement (A + BC -> AC + B): an element replaces another in a compound; use the activity series to determine if the reaction occurs. Double replacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB): ions in two compounds exchange partners; a reaction occurs if one product is an insoluble precipitate (check solubility rules), a gas, or water. Review how to read the activity series and solubility rules from the reference table.

elaborate.description: Predict and classify: Students receive 8 potential reactions. For each, they must: (1) classify the expected reaction type (single or double replacement), (2) predict whether the reaction will occur (using activity series or solubility rules), (3) if it occurs, write and balance the equation and identify any precipitate. Includes 'no reaction' cases to reinforce that not all mixed substances react.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Will magnesium react with hydrochloric acid? Use the activity series to justify your answer and write the balanced equation if it occurs. (2) Predict the products when solutions of sodium sulfate and barium chloride are mixed. Use solubility rules to identify any precipitate. (3) Classify the reaction: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a highlighted activity series with the most common metals starred; include a decision flowchart: 'Is the single element higher on the activity series than the element it would replace? If yes, reaction occurs.' For double replacement, provide a simplified solubility table.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the reaction prediction practice as designed with reference tables.
differentiation.advanced: Write net ionic equations for the double replacement reactions, identifying spectator ions.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual activity series and solubility rules with color-coded categories; include translated instructions and sentence frames for prediction justifications.
differentiation.iep: Reduce prediction problems from 8 to 5; provide a completed example for each reaction type; allow use of all reference tables during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to water quality testing in communities: double replacement reactions are the basis of many water tests — adding reagents that form precipitates with specific contaminants (e.g., adding silver nitrate to test for chloride ions, adding barium chloride to test for sulfate ions). Discuss how communities in places like Flint, Michigan, used these chemistry principles to independently verify lead contamination when official reports were inaccurate.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'activity series': Zinc reacted with copper sulfate solution because___. Copper is below zinc on the activity series, but if we placed copper in zinc sulfate solution, no reaction would occur because___. The activity series ranks metals by their reactivity, so a more active metal will___.

vocabulary.definition: A reaction in which one element replaces another element in a compound (A + BC -> AC + B)
A reaction in which the positive ions of two ionic compounds exchange partners (AB + CD -> AD + CB)
A list of metals ranked by their ability to replace other metals or hydrogen in chemical reactions; more active metals are at the top
A set of guidelines that predict whether an ionic compound will dissolve in water or form an insoluble precipitate
An ion that is present in the reaction solution but does not participate in the reaction

cer.phenomenon: A student places a copper penny into a clear solution of silver nitrate (AgNO3). After 24 hours, the penny is covered with shiny silver crystals and the solution has turned blue. The student places another copper penny into zinc nitrate solution and observes no change after 24 hours.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that copper reacted with silver nitrate but not with zinc nitrate because of its position on the activity series:___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to compare the positions of copper, silver, and zinc, and explain why one reaction occurred and the other did not.
cer.reasoning_frame: On the activity series, the order from most to least active is: Zn > Cu > Ag. Copper replaced silver because copper is___ the activity series than silver. However, copper did not replace zinc because copper is___ the activity series than zinc. The blue color appeared because___, and the silver crystals formed because___.

lessons.title: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can interpret the coefficients in a balanced equation as mole ratios and use them to calculate the amount of product formed from a given amount of reactant.
lessons.circle_prompt: If a recipe for 12 cookies calls for 2 eggs and 3 cups of flour, how many eggs do you need for 36 cookies? What mathematical relationship did you just use?
lessons.do_now: The balanced equation for the formation of water is: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. According to this equation, how many molecules of hydrogen react with each molecule of oxygen? If you had 6 molecules of H2, how many molecules of O2 would you need? How many molecules of H2O would form?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Stoichiometry road map (printed — showing moles A -> mole ratio -> moles B)

engage.description: Recipe analogy: Show a recipe for s'mores: 1 chocolate bar + 2 graham crackers + 1 marshmallow = 1 s'more. If you have 10 chocolate bars, how many graham crackers do you need? How many s'mores can you make? The ratio (1:2:1:1) is fixed by the 'recipe.' In chemistry, the balanced equation IS the recipe, and the coefficients give the ratio.

explore.description: Students practice reading mole ratios from 5 balanced equations. For each equation, they write all possible mole ratios. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives ratios of 2 mol H2 : 1 mol O2, 2 mol H2 : 2 mol H2O, 1 mol O2 : 2 mol H2O. Then they use these ratios to solve basic mole-to-mole problems: 'If 4.0 moles of H2 react, how many moles of H2O are produced?'

explain.description: Teacher introduces stoichiometry as the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced equation. The process: (1) Start with the given amount in moles. (2) Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation as a conversion factor. (3) Get the desired amount in moles. Demonstrate with the airbag reaction: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. If we decompose 5.0 moles of NaN3, how many moles of N2 are produced? (5.0 mol NaN3 x 3 mol N2 / 2 mol NaN3 = 7.5 mol N2)

elaborate.description: Practice problems with increasing complexity: (1) Mole-to-mole: How many moles of CO2 are produced from 3.0 moles of C3H8 in combustion? (2) Connect to the blueberry field cluster: In the equation 2S + 3O2 + 6H2O -> 4H3O+ + 2SO4(2-), if 0.50 moles of sulfur react, how many moles of H3O+ are produced? Students set up each problem using dimensional analysis with the mole ratio clearly shown.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given the balanced equation: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 (the Haber process for making ammonia). (1) Write the mole ratio of H2 to NH3. (2) How many moles of NH3 are produced from 9.0 moles of H2? (3) If a factory needs to produce 100.0 moles of NH3, how many moles of N2 are required?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a mole ratio setup template: '___ mol given x (___ mol desired / ___ mol given) = ___ mol desired' with the balanced equation written above and arrows connecting coefficients to the conversion factor.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mole ratio practice and stoichiometry problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Extend to real-world scale: If the Haber process plant produces 1000 kg of NH3 per day, how many kg of N2 and H2 are consumed daily?
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual stoichiometry road map with color-coded arrows; use the recipe analogy consistently with visual examples; bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems by half; provide a clear mole ratio template; allow use of a completed example as reference; calculator provided.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Haber-Bosch process: Fritz Haber (German-Jewish chemist) developed the process for synthesizing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, which enabled mass production of fertilizers that now feed billions of people. However, the same process was used to manufacture explosives in World War I. This dual-use nature of chemistry raises ethical questions about scientific responsibility. Carl Bosch (German engineer) scaled the process industrially.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'mole ratio': The balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O tells us that 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen because___. The coefficients give the mole ratio but not the mass ratio, so we need to convert between moles and grams because___. If we double the amount of reactants, the amount of products doubles because___.

vocabulary.definition: The calculation of quantities (moles, mass, volume) of reactants and products in a chemical reaction using the balanced equation
The ratio of moles of any two substances in a balanced chemical equation, determined by the coefficients
The number in front of a formula in a balanced equation that represents the number of moles of that substance

Section 2: Mole Ratios — Converting Between Substances
Section 3: Setting Up Mole-to-Mole Stoichiometry Problems
Section 4: Connecting Stoichiometry to Real-World Applications

cer.phenomenon: An airbag contains 130 g of sodium azide (NaN3). The decomposition reaction is: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Engineers need to know exactly how many moles of N2 gas will be produced to ensure the bag inflates to the correct volume.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that 130 g of NaN3 will produce___ moles of N2 gas because___.
cer.evidence_source: Convert grams of NaN3 to moles, then use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of N2 produced.
cer.reasoning_frame: First, the molar mass of NaN3 is___ g/mol, so 130 g / ___ = ___ moles NaN3. The balanced equation shows a mole ratio of___ mol N2 : ___ mol NaN3. So ___ mol NaN3 x ___/___ = ___ moles N2. This is critical for airbag design because___.

lessons.title: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can perform mass-to-mass stoichiometric calculations by converting grams of a given substance to grams of a desired substance using molar mass and mole ratios.
lessons.circle_prompt: When you buy ingredients for a recipe, you measure in grams or cups — not in 'number of molecules.' How do we connect what we measure on a scale to what happens between atoms?
lessons.do_now: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, if you start with 4.0 g of H2, how many grams of water will be produced? Think about what steps you need: grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams. Set up the road map.

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Stoichiometry road map poster (grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams)

engage.description: Connect to the anchoring phenomenon: The airbag contains 130 g of NaN3. We calculated moles of N2 last lesson. But the engineer needs to know the mass of nitrogen gas produced (to calculate volume using gas laws). Today we complete the full calculation: grams of reactant -> grams of product. This is the central skill of stoichiometry.

explore.description: Students solve the airbag problem end-to-end: 130 g NaN3 -> moles NaN3 -> moles N2 -> grams N2. Then they practice with 3 additional problems of increasing difficulty: (1) How many grams of iron are produced from 100.0 g of Fe2O3 in a thermite reaction? (2) How many grams of CO2 are produced when 50.0 g of propane (C3H8) undergoes combustion? (3) Connect to the Regents smartphone cluster: How many grams of Al2O3 are needed to produce 10.32 g of aluminum?

explain.description: Teacher reviews the complete stoichiometry road map: Grams A -> (divide by molar mass A) -> Moles A -> (multiply by mole ratio B/A) -> Moles B -> (multiply by molar mass B) -> Grams B. Emphasize that this can be written as one continuous dimensional analysis chain. Work through the smartphone aluminum problem step by step, showing units cancellation throughout.

elaborate.description: Multi-step application problems: (1) A bakery uses 500 g of baking soda (NaHCO3) in a recipe. When it decomposes during baking (2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2), what mass of CO2 gas makes the bread rise? (2) Reverse problem: How many grams of aluminum must be used to produce 50.0 g of aluminum oxide in the reaction 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: The Haber process: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. (1) How many grams of NH3 can be produced from 28.0 g of N2? (2) How many grams of H2 are needed to react completely with 28.0 g of N2? (3) Verify conservation of mass: add the mass of reactants and compare to the mass of products.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a dimensional analysis template with blanks for each conversion: '___ g A x (1 mol A / ___ g A) x (___ mol B / ___ mol A) x (___ g B / 1 mol B) = ___ g B'; include a completed example next to the template.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mass-to-mass practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve reverse-engineering problems: Given the mass of a product, determine the minimum mass of each reactant needed (connecting to industrial chemistry).
differentiation.ell: Provide a color-coded road map with each step in a different color matching the dimensional analysis template; include bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed dimensional analysis example as a reference; break each problem into 3 numbered steps (grams to moles, mole ratio, moles to grams); allow calculator and all reference materials.

The mole ratio connects reactants to products, so the calculation goes grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams because___. Engineers need stoichiometry to design airbags because___.

A problem-solving method that uses conversion factors arranged so that unwanted units cancel, leaving only the desired units
The exact mole ratio between any two substances in a balanced equation, as determined by the coefficients

cer.phenomenon: A popular smartphone requires 10.32 g of aluminum. The aluminum is extracted from aluminum oxide (Al2O3) using the reaction: 2Al2O3 + 3C -> 4Al + 3CO2. The smartphone manufacturer needs to determine how much aluminum oxide ore to order.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that___ grams of Al2O3 are needed to produce 10.32 g of aluminum for one smartphone because___.
cer.evidence_source: Set up and solve the mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem using the balanced equation, molar masses, and mole ratios. Show all steps of dimensional analysis.
cer.reasoning_frame: Step 1: 10.32 g Al / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Al. Step 2: ___ mol Al x ___ mol Al2O3 / ___ mol Al = ___ mol Al2O3. Step 3: ___ mol Al2O3 x ___ g/mol = ___ g Al2O3. Therefore, the manufacturer needs___ g of aluminum oxide per smartphone, which demonstrates that stoichiometry is essential for___.

lessons.title: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify the limiting reagent in a chemical reaction and calculate the maximum amount of product that can be formed.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever run out of one ingredient while cooking and had leftovers of another? What determined when you had to stop?
lessons.do_now: You have 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese. Each sandwich requires 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. How many sandwiches can you make? What runs out first? What is left over?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

materials: Colored blocks or beads for physical limiting reagent simulation

engage.description: S'mores factory simulation: Give each group 8 graham crackers, 3 marshmallows, and 5 chocolate bars. The recipe: 2 graham crackers + 1 marshmallow + 1 chocolate = 1 s'more. Which ingredient limits production? How many s'mores can they make? What is left over? The limiting ingredient is the 'limiting reagent' in chemistry.

explore.description: Students solve the limiting reagent problem systematically: Given the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, if you have 5.0 moles of H2 and 3.0 moles of O2, which is the limiting reagent? Method: Calculate how much product each reactant could make separately. Whichever makes LESS product is the limiting reagent. H2: 5.0 mol x (2 mol H2O / 2 mol H2) = 5.0 mol H2O. O2: 3.0 mol x (2 mol H2O / 1 mol O2) = 6.0 mol H2O. H2 is limiting (makes less product). Students practice with 3 additional mole-based problems.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the limiting reagent concept: The limiting reagent is consumed first and determines the maximum amount of product. The excess reagent is left over. Two methods to identify: (1) Calculate moles of product from each reactant — the smaller value indicates the limiting reagent. (2) Divide moles of each reactant by its coefficient — the smallest ratio is the limiting reagent. Demonstrate mass-to-mass limiting reagent problem: If 10.0 g of Zn reacts with 15.0 g of HCl (Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2), find the limiting reagent and the mass of H2 produced.

elaborate.description: Application problems: (1) In the airbag reaction (2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2), there is only one reactant so there is no limiting reagent — all NaN3 is consumed. But in the aluminum extraction (2Al2O3 + 3C -> 4Al + 3CO2), if a factory has 500 g of Al2O3 and 100 g of C, which is limiting? How much aluminum is produced? (2) Calculate the mass of excess reagent remaining after the reaction.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: The reaction is: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. If 50.0 g of Fe2O3 reacts with 30.0 g of CO, (1) which is the limiting reagent? (2) What mass of iron is produced? (3) What mass of the excess reagent remains unreacted?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a limiting reagent identification template: 'Reactant A: ___ g -> ___ mol -> makes ___ mol product. Reactant B: ___ g -> ___ mol -> makes ___ mol product. Smaller amount = limiting reagent.' Include the s'mores analogy as a reference throughout.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the limiting reagent practice and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate excess reagent remaining for all problems and verify by showing total mass of all products plus leftover reagent equals total mass of starting materials.
differentiation.ell: Provide the limiting reagent template with visual diagrams and bilingual labels; use the recipe/cooking analogy consistently with culturally familiar foods.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed example with every step labeled; allow use of all reference materials and template during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to resource scarcity: In many industrial processes, one raw material is more expensive or harder to obtain than others. Chemical engineers use limiting reagent calculations to minimize waste and cost. Discuss how pharmaceutical companies in developing countries must optimize reagent use due to supply chain limitations, making stoichiometry a tool for equitable access to medication.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'limiting reagent': The limiting reagent determines the maximum product because___. You might have excess of one reactant, but the reaction stops when the limiting reagent is consumed because___. In the sandwich analogy, bread was the limiting factor, so even though there was extra cheese,___.

vocabulary.definition: The reactant that is completely consumed in a chemical reaction and determines the maximum amount of product that can be formed
The reactant that remains after the limiting reagent is completely consumed; some of it is left over
The maximum amount of product that can be produced from a given amount of limiting reagent, calculated from stoichiometry

cer.phenomenon: A chemistry student mixes 20.0 g of iron filings with 20.0 g of sulfur powder and heats the mixture. The reaction is: Fe + S -> FeS. After the reaction, some yellow sulfur powder is visible in the crucible, but no unreacted iron remains.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that iron is the limiting reagent and sulfur is the excess reagent because___.
cer.evidence_source: Convert both reactants to moles, compare using the 1:1 mole ratio, and identify which is consumed first. Calculate the mass of excess sulfur remaining.
cer.reasoning_frame: 20.0 g Fe / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Fe. 20.0 g S / ___ g/mol = ___ mol S. The 1:1 ratio requires equal moles, but we have more moles of___ than___. So___ is limiting. The excess sulfur remaining is: ___ mol excess x ___ g/mol = ___ g. This explains the visual observation of leftover yellow sulfur because___.

lessons.title: Percent Yield
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the theoretical yield, actual yield, and percent yield of a chemical reaction and explain why actual yield is often less than theoretical yield.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a goal you set for yourself — how close did you get to achieving 100% of it? What factors prevented you from reaching the full goal?
lessons.do_now: A recipe says it makes 24 cookies, but you only got 20. What is your 'percent yield'? (20/24 x 100% = 83.3%) Why might you get fewer cookies than expected?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions

engage.description: Ask: If stoichiometry tells us exactly how much product should form, do real reactions always produce exactly that amount? Show data from a class lab: the theoretical yield of a precipitate was 5.00 g, but students obtained amounts ranging from 3.8 g to 4.7 g. Why? Sources of error: incomplete reactions, side reactions, loss during transfer, impure reagents. The actual amount obtained is called actual yield.

explore.description: Students practice with 4 percent yield problems: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%. (1) A student calculates a theoretical yield of 15.0 g and obtains 12.6 g. What is the percent yield? (2) If the theoretical yield of iron from a reaction is 100.0 g and the percent yield is 85%, what mass of iron was actually obtained? (3) Reverse: If 8.0 g of product was obtained and the percent yield was 80%, what was the theoretical yield?

explain.description: Teacher defines the three yields: Theoretical yield = maximum product possible from stoichiometry (always calculated). Actual yield = amount actually obtained in the lab (always measured). Percent yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100%. Discuss why percent yield is never over 100% in a properly conducted experiment (if it is, something is wrong — impurity, measurement error). Discuss industrial significance: pharmaceutical companies aim for high percent yields to minimize waste and cost.

elaborate.description: Full stoichiometry-to-percent-yield problem: When 15.0 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid (Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2), 0.38 g of hydrogen gas is collected. (1) Calculate the theoretical yield of H2. (2) Calculate the percent yield. (3) Give two reasons why the actual yield might be less than theoretical.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: In the reaction 2Al + 3CuSO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3Cu, a student starts with 5.40 g of aluminum and excess CuSO4. (1) Calculate the theoretical yield of copper. (2) The student actually obtains 17.5 g of copper. Calculate the percent yield. (3) List two factors that could account for the difference between theoretical and actual yield.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a percent yield formula card and a step-by-step template: 'Step 1: Calculate theoretical yield using stoichiometry. Step 2: Record actual yield from lab. Step 3: Divide actual by theoretical and multiply by 100%.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the percent yield practice and full stoichiometry problem as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research industrial percent yields for common processes (Haber process ~15%, aspirin synthesis ~85%) and discuss how engineers improve percent yield through temperature, pressure, and catalyst optimization.
differentiation.ell: Provide the percent yield formula with visual arrow diagrams showing the relationship between the three yields; include bilingual word problems with key vocabulary highlighted.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed stoichiometry example showing how to find theoretical yield; allow use of all reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how percent yield impacts the pharmaceutical industry and access to medication worldwide. A low percent yield means more raw materials are needed, increasing cost and environmental impact. Highlight the work of chemists in developing countries who optimize reaction conditions to produce medications more efficiently and affordably — making life-saving drugs accessible to more people.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'percent yield': The actual yield is usually less than the theoretical yield because___. A percent yield of 100% would mean the reaction was perfect, but this rarely happens because___. Pharmaceutical companies invest in research to increase percent yield, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The maximum amount of product that can be formed from given amounts of reactants, calculated using stoichiometry
The amount of product actually obtained from a chemical reaction in the laboratory
The ratio of actual yield to theoretical yield, expressed as a percentage: (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%

cer.phenomenon: A pharmaceutical company produces aspirin (C9H8O4) by reacting salicylic acid (C7H6O3) with acetic anhydride (C4H6O3): C7H6O3 + C4H6O3 -> C9H8O4 + C2H4O2. Starting with 100.0 g of salicylic acid and excess acetic anhydride, the company obtains 115.2 g of aspirin.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the percent yield of this aspirin synthesis is___%, which means the reaction was___% efficient.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the theoretical yield of aspirin from 100.0 g of salicylic acid using stoichiometry, then calculate the percent yield using the actual yield of 115.2 g.
cer.reasoning_frame: Theoretical yield: 100.0 g C7H6O3 / ___ g/mol = ___ mol x (1 mol aspirin / 1 mol salicylic acid) x ___ g/mol = ___ g aspirin. Percent yield = 115.2 / ___ x 100% = ___%. The reaction achieved___% of the theoretical maximum, and the remaining___% was lost due to___.

lessons.title: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can use the molar volume of a gas at STP (22.4 L/mol) to convert between moles and liters in stoichiometric calculations involving gases.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about blowing up a balloon. How much air does it take to fill it? Is there a way to predict exactly how big a balloon will get from a chemical reaction?
lessons.do_now: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide produces oxygen gas: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2. If 1.0 mole of O2 is produced, the gas occupies 22.4 liters at standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0 degrees C, 1 atm). How many liters would 2.0 moles of O2 occupy?

dci: PS1.B: Chemical Reactions
PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Molar volume reference card (22.4 L/mol at STP)
Extended stoichiometry road map poster (adding liters)

engage.description: Return to the airbag phenomenon: We calculated the moles and grams of N2 gas produced. But the engineer needs to know the VOLUME of the gas — will it fill the airbag? At STP, one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 liters. This is the molar volume. It is the same for ALL gases at STP because gas particles are so far apart that their size does not matter. Today we add volume to our stoichiometry road map.

explore.description: Students practice basic mole-to-volume and volume-to-mole conversions at STP: (1) How many liters does 3.5 moles of N2 occupy at STP? (2) How many moles of gas are in 44.8 L at STP? Then integrate into stoichiometry: (3) In the airbag reaction (2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2), if 2.0 moles of NaN3 decompose, what volume of N2 is produced at STP? (4) What volume of O2 at STP is needed to completely combust 5.0 g of methane?

explain.description: Teacher extends the stoichiometry road map: Grams <-> Moles <-> Mole Ratio <-> Moles <-> Grams, with a new branch: Moles <-> Liters (at STP, multiply by 22.4 L/mol). Important: 22.4 L/mol is only valid at STP. Preview that the combined gas law (Unit 6+) allows calculations at other conditions. Work through a complete problem: How many liters of CO2 at STP are produced by burning 100.0 g of octane (C8H18)?

elaborate.description: Real-world application: (1) Complete the airbag problem end-to-end: 130 g NaN3 -> moles NaN3 -> moles N2 -> liters N2 at STP. Is this enough to fill a typical airbag (~60 L)? (Note: airbags deploy at higher temperatures, so the actual volume is larger — preview of gas laws.) (2) A car engine burns 1.00 kg of octane per trip. What volume of CO2 gas at STP is released into the atmosphere?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) What is the volume of 0.500 moles of any gas at STP? (2) In the reaction CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, what volume of CO2 at STP is produced from the decomposition of 25.0 g of calcium carbonate? (3) Why does molar volume work the same for all gases at STP, regardless of the gas's identity?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the extended road map with the volume branch clearly marked and the conversion factor (22.4 L/mol) pre-printed; include a step-by-step template for gas stoichiometry problems.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the gas stoichiometry practice and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the volume of gas produced at non-STP conditions using the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) for one problem, previewing Unit 6 content.
differentiation.ell: Provide the extended road map with color-coded branches (blue for mass, green for volume, red for particles); bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed example showing the full grams-to-liters pathway; allow use of all reference materials.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to environmental science: The volume of greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels can be calculated using gas stoichiometry. Discuss how these calculations inform climate policy — for example, calculating that burning 1 gallon of gasoline produces approximately 8,887 grams of CO2, which occupies about 4,540 liters at STP. This connects chemistry to environmental justice and the disproportionate impact of air pollution on low-income communities near highways and industrial areas.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'molar volume': At STP, one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 liters because___. Hydrogen gas and carbon dioxide gas have very different molar masses, but one mole of each occupies the same volume at STP because___. We can calculate the volume of gas produced by a reaction, so engineers use stoichiometry to___.

vocabulary.definition: The volume occupied by one mole of any gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP), equal to 22.4 liters
The standard conditions defined as 0 degrees Celsius (273 K) and 1 atmosphere of pressure
Stoichiometric calculations involving gaseous reactants or products, using molar volume to convert between moles and liters at STP

cer.phenomenon: A car airbag must inflate to approximately 60 liters of N2 gas in under 40 milliseconds to protect the driver during a collision. The reaction is: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Engineers need to determine exactly how much sodium azide to include in the airbag module.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the airbag needs approximately___ grams of NaN3 to produce 60 liters of N2 at STP because___.
cer.evidence_source: Work backwards from 60 L of N2 at STP to moles of N2, then use mole ratios to find moles of NaN3, and finally convert to grams.
cer.reasoning_frame: 60 L N2 / 22.4 L/mol = ___ mol N2. Using the mole ratio: ___ mol N2 x (2 mol NaN3 / 3 mol N2) = ___ mol NaN3. Converting to grams: ___ mol x ___ g/mol = ___ g NaN3. Note: In reality, the gas is produced at a much higher temperature than STP, so___, meaning less NaN3 is actually needed because___.

lessons.title: Stoichiometry Unit Review and Regents Exam Preparation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can solve multi-step stoichiometry problems and analyze phenomena-based question clusters integrating reaction types, equation balancing, and quantitative calculations.
lessons.circle_prompt: As we finish this unit, what is one thing about chemical reactions that surprised you or changed the way you see everyday events?
lessons.do_now: Quick review challenge — identify the type of reaction, balance the equation, and find the mole ratio of the first reactant to the first product: (a) _Al + _O2 -> _Al2O3 (b) _CaCO3 -> _CaO + _CO2 (c) _CH4 + _O2 -> _CO2 + _H2O. 3 minutes.

This demonstrates the full power of stoichiometry.

lessons.crse_connection: Culminating CRSE connection: Discuss how the skills learned in this unit — balancing equations, stoichiometric calculations, understanding reaction types — are used by environmental scientists to monitor air and water quality, by agricultural chemists to optimize fertilizer use, and by public health officials to ensure clean drinking water. lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion spanning the entire unit. Start with: 'Reactions transform matter.' Students expand: 'Chemical reactions transform matter by rearranging atoms from reactants into products in predictable patterns that can be represented by balanced equations, quantified through stoichiometric calculations using mole ratios, and verified by the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that the total mass and number of each type of atom remain constant throughout any chemical change.'

vocabulary.definition: The quantitative study of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation, using mole ratios to calculate amounts of substances
The principle that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in a chemical reaction; atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed

cer.phenomenon: A community garden uses ammonium sulfate ((NH4)2SO4) as a fertilizer. The garden coordinator purchases a 50.0 kg bag and wants to know how many moles of nitrogen atoms the garden will receive, and what mass of nitrogen is in the bag.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that 50.0 kg of ammonium sulfate contains___ moles of nitrogen atoms and___ kg of nitrogen because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of (NH4)2SO4, convert 50.0 kg to moles, and use the formula to determine the number of moles and mass of nitrogen. Note that each formula unit contains 2 nitrogen atoms.
cer.reasoning_frame: The molar mass of (NH4)2SO4 is___ g/mol. 50,000 g / ___ = ___ moles of (NH4)2SO4. Each formula unit contains___ nitrogen atoms, so ___ x 2 = ___ moles of nitrogen atoms. Mass of nitrogen: ___ mol x 14.01 g/mol = ___ g = ___ kg. The percent nitrogen is___%, which matches the fertilizer label if it reads '___-0-0.' This calculation helps the coordinator determine how much fertilizer to apply because___.
